Developer guidebook

The control repository's onboarding page, operating guides and AWS setup, collected into one page in reading order. Every section below is converted from the document named above it; where this page and a document differ, the document is the one to follow.

Built from 15 files by tools/build_guidebook.py. The Sources list gives each file's hash, so a stale page can be seen.

Onboarding

What the two repositories are, how the team divides the work, and where to look when something fails. The first-day machine setup is its own chapter, the Day-one checklist.

Onboarding

Source ONBOARDING.md, up to “3. First-day checklist”

What a new developer needs on the first day: what this repository is, how to set up a machine, how to take on work, and where to look when something fails. uv run python tools/onboard_check.py checks most of the first-day checklist on your machine.

This page is not a governed document. The rules it summarises live in CLAUDE.md and the guides under docs/guides/; where this page and those differ, they win.

1. The system in 60 seconds

  • The team works in two repositories. This one, the control repository, holds the ideas, plans, backlog, review records and the agents that move work along. The product repository holds the code that is demonstrated.
  • Work moves through a pipeline: an idea is captured, triaged, grouped into tracks, planned, reviewed, and split into phases in backlog/backlog.yaml. One phase is one session of work.
  • A developer claims a phase on control dev, builds it in a product worktree, and closes it with session-close. A passing gating review by an agent is the approval to merge.
  • Both repositories have dev (where work integrates) and main (one merge per demo release). Phase branches reach dev through a pull request merged with a merge commit.
  • Every session starts with the start skill, which asks for the mode: Planning, Implementing or Validating.
  • Demo: 2026-11-05. Code freeze: 2026-11-03.

Skill names. Each of the plugin's skills runs by its short name, such as /start, unless another command already uses that name. The long form /idea-realization:<skill>, such as /start, always works.

Terms used on this page.

  • Bookkeeping: the small commits that go directly on control dev with no pull request: claims, completions, ideas and workstream claims (OPS-001, section 3), and your own entry in docs/systems.yaml (step 5 below).
  • Lock table: backlog/backlog.yaml on control dev. A phase marked active there is locked by whoever claimed it.
  • Gating review: the agent review in session-close whose passing verdict is the approval to merge. A shadow review runs alongside it and is recorded, but decides nothing.
  • Owner has several meanings. The owner is the person who runs the team's repositories, assigns work and approves plans and merges to main. owner: on a backlog phase is the developer it is assigned to; repository-owner there means it is not assigned to anyone yet. A workstream's owner is the developer who claimed it. owner: on a document or system names the key in docs/systems.yaml's owners map that is responsible for it.

The full account is plugins/idea-realization/docs/two-repositories.md, and the branch and pull request rules are the branching and CI guide (OPS-001).

Source ONBOARDING.md, from “4. Claim your workstream”

4. Claim your workstream

A workstream is a set of paths one developer owns, such as product:web/. The owner lists the workstreams in docs/workstreams.yaml; each developer claims one.

uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py show
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py claim <id>

If show prints nothing, the owner has not defined any workstreams yet; there is nothing to claim, and you can come back to this section when they have.

claim only edits the file. It rewrites the whole file, so a comment in it is dropped; that line in your diff is expected. Commit docs/workstreams.yaml directly on control dev and push at once. If the push is rejected, someone pushed first: git pull --rebase origin dev, run workstreams.py check, and push again if the workstream is still yours. Two claims of different workstreams can still conflict, because claim rewrites the whole file. If the rebase stops on a conflict in docs/workstreams.yaml, keep both sides: each workstream keeps the lines its own claim wrote, whichever side they came from. Never resolve it with --ours or --theirs.

In the first two days each workstream writes the interface documents the others build against. The team workflow guide (OPS-005, sections 1 and 2) has the details.

5. Pick a mode with /start

Before every session, in the primary checkout of each repository: git pull --rebase origin dev. The --rebase keeps an unpushed bookkeeping commit on top instead of making a merge commit on dev.

Then run /start and choose a mode:

ModeWhat you doGuide
PlanningTurn captured ideas into approved plans and backlog phasesdocs/guides/OPS-002-planning-mode.md
ImplementingClaim one phase, build it, verify it, merge itdocs/guides/OPS-003-implementing-mode.md
ValidatingReview a plan, a peer's branch, infrastructure or spend; change nothingdocs/guides/OPS-004-validating-mode.md

The one-page versions are in docs/guides/OPS-009-mode-cheat-sheets.md; prompts to paste for each mode are in docs/guides/OPS-010-day-one-prompts.md.

6. Your first phase, end to end

The implementing-mode guide (OPS-003) is the full procedure. In short:

  1. /start, choose Implementing. Pull dev first.
  2. /idea-realization:backlog: see the ready queue. Take the first ready phase in next_up order, preferring one assigned to you (owner: <your handle>).
  3. /idea-realization:session-start: it asks before claiming, then commits the claim directly on control dev and pushes at once, and cuts agent/<phase-id> worktrees in both repositories from origin/dev.
  4. Add the product worktree to the session: /add-dir <product worktree>. Run the product's tests once before changing anything.
  5. Build inside the phase's declared systems and deliverables. Commit small diffs. Push your own branch whenever you like.
  6. /idea-realization:checkpoint whenever you stop: it records progress and never marks the phase complete.
  7. Run every command in the phase's verification list and keep the real output.
  8. Record what the next session should know in the brain (/idea-realization:brain), in the control worktree, so the entry reaches dev in the phase's control pull request.
  9. /idea-realization:session-close: rebases both branches, runs the gating review, opens and merges both pull requests with merge commits, and writes the completion commit on control dev.

7. Daily cadence

Morning sync (pull dev with --rebase, the owner ranks and assigns, agents claim), midday integration (rebase open branches onto origin/dev, merge what passed review), end of day (close or checkpoint every phase, record learnings in the brain, push every branch). The table is in OPS-005, section 5.

8. Rules that bite

  • Pull origin dev with --rebase before any work, and push right after any claim or bookkeeping commit. An unpushed claim lets two people claim the same phase.
  • Every session works in its own worktree. The primary checkout's branch is never switched.
  • Never write a confidential identifier into a tracked file: no organization or client name, account id or repository URL in code, documents or commit messages. Your work email is not confidential: it belongs in your own docs/systems.yaml entry (section 3, step 5) and nowhere else.
  • Never commit with --no-verify, never force-push dev or main, never route around a hook. A failing check is a result to fix or report.
  • Every AWS command goes through tools/aws-sandbox. No default profile, no AWS_ variables, no bare aws. Only the aws-deploy agent writes; every delete asks a person.
  • A backlog/backlog.yaml conflict is normal: keep both sides. Never resolve it with --ours or --theirs.
  • Build against merged interfaces and mocks, never against a peer's unmerged branch.
  • Never edit CLAUDE.md without the owner's approval of that change.
  • A new ask that comes up mid-session is recorded as an idea (/idea-realization:idea), not folded into the phase in progress.
  • The control repository's CI fails when the DENY_LIST secret is missing. The owner sets it; tell the owner if CI reports it absent.

9. Help

  • Something failed: the troubleshooting guide (docs/guides/OPS-008-troubleshooting.md) covers rejected pushes, backlog conflicts, doctor drift, hook refusals, pull request and CI failures, AWS access errors and port clashes.
  • Why was something decided, and what does a term mean: the brain. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/brain.py load --query <word>, or brain/index.md.
  • Demo day: docs/guides/OPS-006-demo-day-runbook.md. AWS cost: docs/guides/OPS-007-cost-guardrails.md.
  • Anything else: ask the owner. Raise a blocker or question with the issue templates in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/.

Team workflow (OPS-005)

Source docs/guides/OPS-005-team-workflow.md, up to “3. Claims”

How a team of developers works in this repository, each on their own machine and each running their own agents. It adds no mechanism: it says how the existing pieces fit together for a team. The rules behind it are in the plugin's protocol documents, which this guide points to rather than repeats:

  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/workstreams.md: workstreams and developer handles;
  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/backlog-protocol.md: claims, concurrency, completion, collisions;
  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/two-repositories.md: the control and product repositories;
  • the branching and CI guide (OPS-001): branch names, pull requests, merge commits, rulesets, CI checks, tags. The git mechanics of every step below are there.

Both repositories have two long-lived branches: dev, where finished work integrates, and main, which receives dev once per demo release. "Control dev" and "product dev" below name the dev branch of each repository.

1. Before the first day's work

Each developer, once:

  1. Add a developer entry to the owners map in docs/systems.yaml: the key is your handle (lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter, at most sixteen characters), the value lists your git author emails. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/identity.py prints the handle your git email resolves to.

    owners:
  ana:
    description: Ana, user interface workstream.
    emails: ["<handle>@<work-domain>"]

  2. Claim one workstream. The owner writes the list of workstreams in docs/workstreams.yaml; developers claim them. A workstream is a set of paths one developer owns, such as product:web/. Other developers' phases keep their deliverables out of it unless the phase records your approval (cross_workstream).

    uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py show
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py claim <id>

    claim edits the file and never commits. Commit only docs/workstreams.yaml on control dev in the primary checkout and push at once. If the push is rejected, someone pushed first: git pull --rebase, run workstreams.py check, and push again if the workstream is still yours; if a peer took it, choose another. If the rebase stops on a conflict in docs/workstreams.yaml, keep both sides: each workstream keeps the lines its own claim wrote. Never resolve it with --ours or --theirs.

The developer entry and the workstream claim are bookkeeping, so they go directly to control dev, not through a pull request.

2. Interfaces first (the first two days)

During the first two days each workstream writes the documents that state what it provides to the others: an architecture document (ARCH) or a decision (ADR) per interface, such as the API's request and response shapes, the event formats between the agent orchestration and the backend, or the data the infrastructure exposes. List them under the workstream's interfaces in docs/workstreams.yaml.

From then on:

  • Build against merged contracts and mocks, never against a peer's branch. If the API is not built yet, the user interface builds against a mock that follows the merged interface document.
  • A peer's unmerged branch can be rebased, rewritten or abandoned; work built on it breaks when it does. Only what is on dev is a contract (backlog-protocol.md, section 7).
  • Changing an interface is a change to its document, merged first, so every consumer sees it before the code that depends on it.

Working modes

Every session starts with /start and one of three modes. This chapter has the guide for each mode and the one-page cheat sheets.

CLAUDE.md

Source CLAUDE.md, from “Pick your mode” up to “Two repositories”

Pick your mode

Start every session with /start (long form /idea-realization:start). The project settings load the plugin, so a plain claude started in this repository has it once you trust the folder. It asks which mode you are in and points you to that mode's guide and first step. The one-page list of steps per mode is the mode cheat sheets (OPS-009); where a cheat sheet and a guide differ, the guide wins.

ModeUse it toMain stepsGuide
Planningturn ideas into approved plans and assigned phasesidea, idea-triage, partition-ideas, idea-planner, plan-adversary, phase-splitter, batch-validatorOPS-002
Implementingbuild one claimed phasebacklog, session-start, build in the product worktree, session-closeOPS-003
Validatingreview plans, branches, infrastructure and spendphase-adversary, plan-adversary, validator-code, aws-infra-reviewer, aws-cost-optimizerOPS-004

Reviewers in Validating mode change nothing they review.

Assignment. The owner assigns a phase by setting owner: <handle> on it and orders the queue in next_up. The repository check warns, and does not refuse, when someone other than the phase's owner claims it.

Planning mode (OPS-002)

Source docs/guides/OPS-002-planning-mode.md, whole document

How a captured idea becomes an approved plan, registered backlog phases and a validated, assigned batch. This guide gives the order of the steps, what each step takes and produces, and who decides at each gate. The rules themselves are in the plugin's protocol documents, which this guide points to rather than repeats:

  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/role-contracts.md: what each role receives, produces and never does, and the decisions reserved to the owner (section 1);
  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/plan-review.md: the plan review (sections 1 to 3);
  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/backlog-protocol.md: phases, next_up and splitting (sections 2, 4, 5 and 14);
  • plugins/idea-realization/docs/batches.md: batches and their check.

The one-page list of commands for this mode is in the mode cheat sheets (OPS-009). How the team's day is organised around it is in the team workflow (OPS-005).

Starting

Run /start and choose Planning. Then, in the control repository's primary checkout on dev:

  1. git pull --rebase origin dev, before any work (OPS-001, section 2).
  2. Load what is already decided: the brain skill, or uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/brain.py load --kind decision.

Plugin skills are invoked as /idea-realization:<skill>. Agents are dispatched by name as their own agent type, never as a general-purpose agent. Run scripts from the control repository's root; they find it from git and need no IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT. If a script resolves the wrong root, set the variable on that one command (IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run ...) and never export it: an exported value makes uv run pytest fail (OPS-001, section 7; OPS-008, "check.py reports files from the wrong repository").

Terms used below. A gate is a stop where the owner decides before the work goes on; the partition step has four (the open-set gate, when open ideas exist, then gates 1, 2 and 3). A disposition is a recorded answer: for a track, whether it becomes a new plan or amends a named one; for a review finding, how it was settled. An altitude is the level a plan review looks at: the plan, each phase, or each later-added phase (step 7). <staging_dir> is the gitignored working directory that paths.py prints.

Where the work is committed

WhatWhere it goes
Idea log entries (new ideas, status moves, findings)Directly on control dev and pushed at once. Idea commits are bookkeeping (OPS-001, section 3).
Accepted partition record, requirement, plan, new phases in backlog/backlog.yaml, batch record in backlog/batches.yaml, regenerated catalogA control worktree on a branch agent/<handle>-<slug>, reaching control dev through a pull request merged with a merge commit (OPS-001, sections 1 and 4). The owner merges planning pull requests.

1. Ideation

/idea-realization:idea records the idea as given, through the plugin's writer, and re-renders the idea view. Record one idea per distinct ask. Do not edit ideas/ideas.jsonl by hand, and read an idea's current state with uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/idea.py show <id>, never from the raw log.

2. Triage

/idea-realization:idea-triage <id> handles one open idea per run. If no id is given it lists the open ideas and asks which one. It dispatches the idea-triage agent with the literal write command, re-reads the idea to confirm the finding is on the right idea, and only then moves the idea to triaged. It never moves an idea past triaged.

3. Partition

/idea-realization:partition-ideas builds the corpus, dispatches two analysts and two audits, and writes one proposed partition. It stops for the owner:

  • at the open-set gate, when open ideas exist: triage them first, or partition without them;
  • at gate 1, after the analysts report;
  • at gate 2, after the first audit;
  • at gate 3, where the owner accepts or corrects the partition and rules on each decline candidate.

Only on the owner's acceptance does idea_corpus.py accept copy the record into the partitions directory with state: accepted. The skill moves no idea's status. Each accepted track carries a disposition: a new plan, or an amendment to a named existing plan.

4 and 5. Codes, then the planner

Reserve the codes first with /idea-realization:next-code plan (and requirement for a new plan). Then dispatch the idea-planner agent with the accepted track and the reserved codes. It refuses to work from a partition still in proposal, from a track without a disposition, or without a reserved code. It writes the requirement under docs/requirements/ and the plan under docs/plans/, both status: draft, and runs the plan check on its own draft before it reports.

6 and 7. Plan check and plan review

/idea-realization:plan-check <plan path> is the entry check: it reads headings only. On a pass, dispatch plan-adversary with the prompt from adversary-prompt.md, once per altitude, every placeholder filled with an absolute path:

  • plan: the plan against its requirement;
  • phase: each queued or blocked phase of the plan, in isolation;
  • later-added-phase: phases added after the plan's original set, against the plan as it stands. Once any later-added phase exists this altitude runs even when the other two came back clean.

The session that dispatches the review records every finding, unchanged, in its session record under ## Review (plan-review.md, section 3, steps 4 and 5). The planner writes a disposition on each: fixed, accepted-no-change, rejected or escalated. There is one revision cycle; a blocker still open after it is escalated.

Gate: plan approval. The owner reads the plan, the review record and the escalated findings, writes dispositions on the escalated ones, and approves the plan by setting status: approved. Nothing later in this guide runs on a draft plan.

8. Phase split

Dispatch the phase-splitter agent with the repository root, the approved plan's code and path, its requirement, the dispositioned review record and the output directory <staging_dir>/phase-split/<plan-code>/ (paths.py prints staging_dir; it is gitignored). It:

  • reuses existing phases that already cover part of the plan;
  • writes one-session phases with every field the backlog schema requires, status: queued, no agent, and owner set to the plan's owner;
  • maps depends_on, computes stages, and records prerequisites outside the plan as external_dependencies;
  • runs check.py and batch_check.py against its candidate files and pastes their output into proposal.md.

It never edits the real backlog or batches file, never ranks next_up and never assigns a developer. Phases it split go back to plan-adversary at the phase altitude before step 9.

9. Batch validation

Dispatch the batch-validator agent with the root, the batch id and, for a proposal, the candidate files from step 8. It runs, from the control repository's root:

uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/batch_check.py --backlog-path <candidate backlog> \
  --batches <candidate batches> <batch-id>
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py --feature backlog --feature batches \
  --backlog-path <candidate backlog>

batch_check.py exits 0 when the composition is clean, 1 when it lists problems, and 2 when a file could not be read or the batch does not exist. The agent then judges what the script does not: that the batch record restates no phase content, that each stage boundary rests on a real edge or collision, that a stage wider than the free active slots will run serially, and that each phase fits one session. Its first line is VERDICT: pass <batch-id> or VERDICT: reject <batch-id>.

10. Assignment

The owner, on the planning branch:

  1. Copies the accepted phases into backlog/backlog.yaml (only the new phases, not the candidate file as a whole) and the batch into backlog/batches.yaml.
  2. Ranks next_up. The splitter's order is a proposal only (backlog-protocol.md, section 4).
  3. Sets owner: <handle> on each phase to assign it to a developer. Anyone may still claim the phase; the check prints a warning when the claimant is not the phase's owner and never refuses the claim (OPS-005, "Assignment").
  4. Sets the batch's status: approved and adds an entry to its checks list from a fresh run of batch_check.py <batch-id> against the real files: date, result, backlog_commit and the output verbatim. The batch-validator never writes this entry; the planning session does.
  5. Runs /idea-realization:catalog, then IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py, and inspects plan coverage with uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/cli.py ready --all (its "Source plan coverage" table): every draft, approved or active plan is covered by at least one phase.

The branch then goes to control dev through a pull request (OPS-001, section 4).

When planning mode ends

Planning mode for a plan ends when all of these hold:

  • the plan is status: approved, with every review finding dispositioned;
  • its phases are registered in backlog/backlog.yaml on control dev;
  • check.py passes on control dev;
  • each batch is status: approved in backlog/batches.yaml, with a recorded passing check;
  • each phase the owner wants built next is in next_up with an owner: <handle>.

From there the work moves to implementing mode (OPS-003).

What planning mode never does

  • No agent approves an idea, accepts a partition, approves a plan, ranks next_up, composes a batch or assigns a developer. Those are the owner's (role-contracts.md, section 1).
  • No step chooses a document code by hand.
  • No step claims a phase. Claiming happens in implementing mode.

Implementing mode (OPS-003)

Source docs/guides/OPS-003-implementing-mode.md, whole document

How one developer's agent takes one queued phase from the backlog to merged code and a completion record. The procedures are the session-start, checkpoint and session-close skills; this guide gives their order, what each leaves behind, and where the AWS agents fit. Git and GitHub mechanics are in the branching and CI guide (OPS-001); claims, review and merge for a team are in the team workflow (OPS-005); the one-page command list is in the mode cheat sheets (OPS-009).

The two repositories

The control repository (this one) holds the backlog, plans, session and review records. The product repository holds the code; its remote is set per machine as product_remote in the untracked .idea-realization/local.yaml. A session has a worktree in each, both on a branch named agent/<phase-id> (plugins/idea-realization/docs/two-repositories.md).

WhatWhere
The claim commit and the completion commitControl primary checkout, directly on control dev, pushed at once
Code, tests, verification commandsProduct worktree, <product worktree dir>/<phase-id>
Session record, checkpoints, review verdict recordsControl worktree, <worktree dir>/<phase-id>

Neither primary checkout ever leaves dev.

The steps

1. Start

Run /start and choose Implementing. In the control primary checkout, git pull --rebase origin dev before anything else, and load the context the phase needs with the brain skill.

2. Choose a phase: backlog skill

/idea-realization:backlog runs the check, shows the ready queue with its Conflicts column, and orients on one phase without claiming it. Take the first ready phase in next_up order, preferring one assigned to you (owner: <handle>). If the check fails, stop: nothing is claimed on a red backlog.

3. Claim and set up: session-start skill

/idea-realization:session-start does, in order:

  1. Pulls origin dev in the control primary checkout.
  2. Asks before claiming, reporting the phase, its conflicts, whether its deliverables sit in your workstream, and anything that looked wrong.
  3. On a yes, edits only this phase's lines (status: active, agent: <handle>/agent-<name>), regenerates the catalog, runs the check, commits directly on control dev and pushes at once. The check refuses a claim that overlaps an active phase's systems, deliverable paths or dependency chain, that exceeds max_active, or that falls inside another developer's workstream without their recorded approval. It warns, and does not refuse, when the phase's owner: is a different developer: ask that developer before going on. A rejected push means a peer pushed first: git pull --rebase, re-run the check, push again if the claim is still safe.
  4. Cuts agent/<phase-id> from origin/dev in both repositories, each in its own worktree outside the repository.
  5. Asks you to add the product worktree to the session with /add-dir <product worktree dir>/<phase-id> (or start the next session with claude --add-dir <product worktree dir>/<phase-id> from the control worktree).
  6. Has you install the product worktree's own environment and run the product's tests once before any change, keeping the output.

Output: an active phase pushed on control dev, two worktrees, a baseline test run.

4. Build in the product worktree
  • Stay inside the phase's systems and deliverables. A deliverable written product:<path> is a path in the product worktree. If the work needs a file outside them, stop, and widen the declaration on control dev first so peers see the wider lock.
  • Commit narrow diffs on agent/<phase-id>. Rebase onto origin/dev whenever a peer integrates; never merge dev in.
  • Push your own agent/<phase-id> branches whenever you like; that needs no approval.
  • Build against merged interfaces and mocks, never against a peer's unmerged branch (OPS-005, section 2).
  • Pick a free port explicitly for any dev server.
  • Record new asks as ideas with the idea skill; do not fold them into the phase.
5. Record progress: checkpoint skill

/idea-realization:checkpoint writes the session record in the control worktree: the phase, the verification output, an acceptance verdict per condition, the backlog fields, and what is unresolved. It is safe to repeat and never marks a phase complete.

Current limitation: the checkpoint skill is still written for one repository. It edits and runs verification only in the working tree it is run from, and does not record the product branch's state. Its two-repository version is the queued phase Checkpoint skill for two repositories (phase-boot-14), whose acceptance is that a checkpoint records both branches' tips. Until it lands:

  • run checkpoint from the control worktree;
  • run the phase's product verification commands in the product worktree yourself, so the ## Verification section holds their real output, not a summary;
  • when you hand off, make sure the product agent/<phase-id> branch is pushed and that next_action says what remains in the product repository.
6. AWS work, when the phase has any

All AWS access goes through tools/aws-sandbox with the two sandbox profiles; no machine holds a default profile or ambient credentials. Check the machine once with uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe and tools/aws-sandbox whoami.

NeedAgentWhat it does
Calling Claude through Amazon Bedrockbedrock-claude-advisorRead-only. Which models and inference profiles the sandbox can call in its region, request shapes, quotas, prompt caching, streaming and tool use, checked against the account and current documentation. Ask before writing Bedrock calls, not after.
Reviewing an infrastructure diff before it is deployedaws-infra-reviewerRead-only. Ranked findings on IAM scope, exposure, encryption, secrets, tags, alarms and idle cost (OPS-004).
Deploying the change to the sandboxaws-deployThe only agent that creates or updates AWS resources. Runs on your machine with the deploy role, states its plan, shows a diff or change set before applying, asks a person to approve every deletion, and reads back what it changed. Deploy is local only; no CI workflow deploys (OPS-001).
Checking what is running and why it is notaws-ops-inspectorRead-only. Health, logs, alarms and recent errors, with the real output.

Tag every resource with project and owner (OPS-007, "Tags"). Keep the deploy report and the inspector's output in the session record: they are evidence for acceptance conditions about the deployed system.

7. Verify

Run every command in the phase's verification list and keep the real output. A command runs in the product worktree unless it starts with control:, which runs in the control worktree. A failing check is a result to record, not a step to retry until it passes. session-close runs the verification again after rebasing, and that run is the one the review judges.

8. Close: session-close skill

/idea-realization:session-close is the only procedure that marks a phase complete. It:

  1. Runs the checkpoint steps against the current state.
  2. Rebases both branches onto origin/dev, runs the verification and the control check.
  3. Runs the gating review: a fresh phase-adversary agent (or validator-code for a narrow code change against one requirement) judges the product diff against the phase's acceptance. The review and the shadow review-judge are described in validating mode (OPS-004).
  4. Records the verdict under docs/reviews/ in the control worktree, with reviewed_commit set to the product HEAD that was judged. Every finding is fixed (with a fresh review of the new HEAD) or accepted by the developer who owns the workstream. Two rejects on the same finding: stop and report to the owner.
  5. On a passing verdict, pushes both branches, opens a pull request to dev in each repository, merges the control pull request, waits for the product's required check verify, then merges the product pull request. Both are merge commits, pinned with --match-head-commit. The passing gating review is the approval for both merges; no separate approval is asked for.
  6. Confirms the product merge commit's second parent equals reviewed_commit and that the merge is on product dev.
  7. Writes the completion commit directly on control dev: status: complete, session, completion_evidence, product_merge: <merge commit>, result, the phase removed from next_up, the catalog regenerated, the check run, git pull --rebase, then push. If the push fails after the product merged, retry; never revert the product merge. The phase stays active until this commit lands.
  8. Removes both worktrees and both local branches, copying out any ignored content first.

A repository with no origin, or a local-path one, uses a local git merge --no-ff instead; a hosted origin that gh cannot reach stops the close rather than merging locally. The skill says which path applied. Commands for each step and the failure cases are in OPS-001, section 4, and OPS-008.

Before you run session-close, record what the next session should know with the brain skill, as a lesson or a decision, in the control worktree. The entry and brain/index.md are committed on agent/<phase-id> and reach dev in the control pull request.

How implementing mode ends

A session ends in one of two states:

  • Complete and merged. The gating review passed, both pull requests merged with merge commits, the second-parent check held, and the completion commit is on control dev.
  • Released with a next_action. Any condition is unmet: verification is red, the review rejected, or the work is unfinished. Run checkpoint. If someone will continue, the phase stays active; if nobody is continuing it, return it to queued, clear agent, session, completion_evidence and result in the same edit, and write a next_action that names exactly what remains, including anything the review found. Push both feature branches so no work exists only on one machine. Closing honestly incomplete is a correct outcome.

Validating mode (OPS-004)

Source docs/guides/OPS-004-validating-mode.md, up to “Phase reviews”

How plans, phase branches, infrastructure and spend are reviewed, which reviewer does each, and what a reviewer's verdict decides. Reviewers change nothing: every reviewer agent below is read-and-run only and spawns no subagents. The one-page command list is in the mode cheat sheets (OPS-009).

Run /start and choose Validating. Then git pull --rebase origin dev in the control primary checkout before any work.

The rules every review follows

  • A fresh agent of a dedicated reviewer type. Never a fork of the session that did the work, which carries its conclusions, and never a general-purpose agent.
  • Evidence, not rationale. A verdict rests on commands the reviewer ran and their real output, or on diff hunks. The builder's explanation is not evidence (plugins/idea-realization/docs/role-contracts.md, section 2).
  • Every verdict on a phase diff is recorded as a JSON file under docs/reviews/, named <date>-<phase-id>-<reviewer type>.json, valid against .idea-realization/schemas/review-verdict.schema.json. reviewed_commit is the full commit the reviewer judged; gating is true when the verdict decided the merge and false when it ran in shadow. Findings are copied as written.
  • Every finding is fixed or accepted by the developer who owns the workstream it is in, with the disposition recorded. A fix that changes the diff needs a fresh review of the new commit.

Which reviewer, when

What is reviewedReviewerWhenWhat its verdict decides
A phase's product diffphase-adversaryEvery phase, in session-close step 3Gating: the phase may merge only on a pass
A narrow code change against one requirementvalidator-codeInstead of phase-adversary, when the phase is that narrowGating
The same phase diffreview-judgeBeside every gating reviewNothing: shadow only
Mechanical gates on a branchvalidator-checkBefore a gating review, or whenever a branch's checks need runningPass or fail per gate; no judgement
An infrastructure diffaws-infra-reviewerEvery phase whose diff changes infrastructure code, before aws-deploy applies itRanked findings; each is fixed or accepted like any other finding
Sandbox spend and idle resourcesaws-cost-optimizerOnce per working dayRecommendations only (OPS-007)
A plan and its requirementplan-adversaryEach new plan, at three altitudesFindings for the planner's dispositions; approval stays with the owner
A batch compositionbatch-validatorEach proposed batch, before the owner approves itEvidence for the owner; not approval

Source docs/guides/OPS-004-validating-mode.md, from “Infrastructure and spend” up to “Reviewing a peer's ready branch”

Infrastructure and spend

aws-infra-reviewer

Dispatch it for every phase whose product diff touches infrastructure code, before aws-deploy applies the change, with the diff and the phase's acceptance or requirement. It reads the sandbox through tools/aws-sandbox with the read role, compares live resources with the code where the change is already deployed, and reports ranked findings: IAM scope, public exposure, encryption, secrets, tags, alarms and logging, idle cost, and resources a later deploy would replace. Findings are fixed or accepted by the workstream's owner, like gating findings. It does not replace the gating review of the phase.

aws-cost-optimizer

Once per working day, a validator dispatches it with the prompt in OPS-007, "Daily cost review", posts the spend and the idle-resource list to the team, and each resource's owner keeps it with a reason or asks aws-deploy to remove it.

Plan and batch reviews

  • Plans: plan-adversary, once per altitude (plan, phase, later-added-phase), with the filled prompt from plugins/idea-realization/docs/adversary-prompt.md, after the plan passes the plan-check skill. The procedure and the review record are in plugins/idea-realization/docs/plan-review.md, section 3; the order within planning is in OPS-002.
  • Queued phases under a review pack: a review session working under a prompt pack the owner approved may edit the in-scope queued phases' backlog lines, never next_up, status or agent (plan-review.md, section 4, and plugins/idea-realization/docs/prompt-packs.md).
  • Batches: batch-validator, which runs plugins/idea-realization/scripts/batch_check.py <batch-id> and the repository check, then judges the rules in plugins/idea-realization/docs/batches.md. Its first line is VERDICT: pass <batch-id> or VERDICT: reject <batch-id>.

Mode cheat sheets (OPS-009)

Source docs/guides/OPS-009-mode-cheat-sheets.md, whole document

One page per mode: the skills, agents and commands in the order they are used, one line each. The full procedure for each mode is in its guide: planning (OPS-002), implementing (OPS-003), validating (OPS-004). Where this page and a guide differ, the guide wins. Prompts to paste for each mode are in OPS-010.

Entry point for every mode: /start (long form /idea-realization:start). It asks which mode you are in and points to that mode's first step.

Plugin skills are invoked as /idea-realization:<skill>. Agents are dispatched by name, never as a general-purpose agent. Run scripts from the control repository's root; they find it from git and need no IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT. If a script resolves the wrong root, set the variable on that one command (IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run ...) and never export it: an exported value makes uv run pytest fail (OPS-001, section 7; OPS-008, "check.py reports files from the wrong repository").

Planning

From a captured idea to approved plans, registered phases and validated, assigned batches.

  1. /start, choose Planning.
  2. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/brain.py load --kind decision — read what is already decided.
  3. /idea-realization:idea — record each new idea as given.
  4. /idea-realization:idea-triage <id> — scout one open idea for related material; moves it to triaged.
  5. /idea-realization:partition-ideas — group triaged ideas into tracks; stops for the owner at each gate.
  6. /idea-realization:next-code plan (and requirement) — reserve the codes first; never choose one by hand.
  7. idea-planner agent — drafts the requirement and plan for one accepted track, with the reserved codes.
  8. /idea-realization:plan-check <plan> — check the plan has the sections it needs.
  9. plan-adversary agent — attacks the plan at three altitudes (plugins/idea-realization/docs/plan-review.md, section 3).
  10. phase-splitter agent — splits the approved plan into one-session phases with systems, deliverables and dependencies.
  11. batch-validator agent and scripts/batch_check.py — confirm each batch is dependency-closed and collision-free.
  12. Owner — orders next_up and sets owner: <handle> on each phase.
  13. /idea-realization:catalog, then uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py — must pass before the commit.

Done when: the plan is approved, its phases are registered, the check passes, and each batch is validated and assigned.

Implementing

From a claimed phase to merged code and a completion record.

  1. /start, choose Implementing.
  2. git pull --rebase origin dev on control dev — always, before any work.
  3. /idea-realization:brain — load the context the phase needs.
  4. /idea-realization:backlog — run the check, see the ready queue and its Conflicts column, orient on one phase.
  5. /idea-realization:session-start — claim the phase (push the claim at once), cut both agent/<phase-id> branches and worktrees.
  6. /add-dir <product worktree> — add the product worktree to the session.
  7. Build and test in the product worktree; commit narrow diffs; rebase onto origin/dev, never merge it in.
  8. /idea-realization:checkpoint — record progress as often as useful; it never completes a phase.
  9. bedrock-claude-advisor agent — model ids, quotas and request shapes for Bedrock calls; read-only.
  10. aws-infra-reviewer agent — review any infrastructure diff before it is deployed (OPS-004).
  11. aws-deploy agent — deploy the change to the sandbox; the only agent that creates or updates AWS resources.
  12. aws-ops-inspector agent — read the deployed resources' state and errors.
  13. /idea-realization:brain — record what the next session should know, as a lesson or decision, in the control worktree before closing.
  14. /idea-realization:session-close — verification, gating review, pull requests merged with merge commits, completion record on control dev.

Done when: the phase is complete and merged in both repositories, or handed back with an exact next_action.

Validating

Reviewing plans, branches, infrastructure and spend. Reviewers change nothing.

  1. /start, choose Validating.
  2. phase-adversary agent — the gating review of a phase's product diff; session-close dispatches it with the phase's acceptance.
  3. validator-code agent — gating review instead, for a narrow code change judged against one requirement.
  4. review-judge agent — shadow judge of the same diff, dispatched by a session other than the one that built the phase (session-close does not run it); its verdict is recorded and decides nothing.
  5. validator-check agent — runs the mechanical checks on a branch.
  6. aws-infra-reviewer agent — reviews every infrastructure diff for security, reliability, cost and fit.
  7. aws-cost-optimizer agent — daily spend and idle-resource review (OPS-007).
  8. plan-adversary agent — plan reviews at three altitudes (plugins/idea-realization/docs/plan-review.md, section 3).
  9. Queued-phase review packs — plugins/idea-realization/docs/plan-review.md, section 4.
  10. Smoke test of each release candidate (OPS-006).

Every verdict is recorded under docs/reviews/ with its reviewed_commit; every finding is fixed or accepted by the workstream's owner, with the disposition recorded.

Branching and pull-request flow

Branch names, how a phase's branches reach dev in both repositories, and the CI jobs and rulesets that guard them.

Branching and CI (OPS-001)

Source docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, up to “3. What goes direct to control dev”

How branches, pull requests, merges, release tags and GitHub CI work in the control repository (this one) and the product repository.

Deploy is local only for now. No workflow here deploys anything. A developer deploys to the AWS sandbox from their own machine with the aws-deploy agent. A draft plan for deploying from GitHub Actions to AWS through OIDC is PLAN-002 (docs/plans/PLAN-002-ci-deploy-to-aws.md); until the owner accepts it, CI only verifies.

1. Branches

Both repositories have the same two long-lived branches:

BranchRole
devIntegration branch and the default branch. Every finished phase lands here.
mainRelease branch. Changes only through a release pull request from dev.

Short-lived branches:

NameUseMerged?
agent/<phase-id>A claimed phase. The same name in both repositories.Yes, to dev by pull request
agent/<handle>-<slug>Work the owner directed that has no claimed phase. <handle> is the developer's handle.Yes, to dev by pull request
spike/<handle>-<slug>An experiment.Never. Delete it or keep it unmerged.

Cut every feature branch from origin/dev in both repositories. A hotfix is a phase, not a branch type (section 6).

Force-pushing. A feature branch may be force-pushed with git push --force-with-lease after it has been rebased onto origin/dev; session-close does this before it opens the pull request. dev and main are never force-pushed, and the rulesets refuse it (section 9). Plain --force is not used on any branch.

2. Before any work, and after any bookkeeping

  • Always git pull --rebase origin dev before starting any work, in both repositories. --rebase keeps an unpushed bookkeeping commit on top instead of making a merge commit on dev.
  • Push right after a claim commit or any other bookkeeping commit. An unpushed claim is invisible to the rest of the team and lets two people claim the same phase.

Source docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, from “4. Merging a phase: pull request with a merge commit” up to “5. Releases: dev to main, and demo tags”

4. Merging a phase: pull request with a merge commit

Feature branches reach dev only through a pull request merged with a merge commit. Squash and rebase merges are switched off in both repositories, because they create new commits and the reviewed commit would no longer be in dev's history.

The passing gating review is the approval for both merges. No separate owner approval is needed per merge, and the rulesets require 0 approving reviews.

The sequence, as session-close runs it:

  1. Rebase both feature branches onto origin/dev; run verification and the gating review.

  2. Push both feature branches. Open (or reuse) a pull request to dev in each repository: gh pr create --base dev.

  3. Control pull request: gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <control HEAD>.

  4. Product pull request: wait for the required check verify (gh pr checks <n> --watch), then gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <reviewed_commit>. --match-head-commit makes GitHub refuse the merge if the branch head moved after the review.

  5. Second-parent check. Fetch, then confirm in the product repository:

    git fetch origin
git rev-parse <merge commit>^2    # must equal reviewed_commit

    The pull request head, the merge commit's second parent and the gating verdict's reviewed_commit must be the same commit. If they differ, stop and report it.

  6. Completion commit direct to control dev (section 3): status: complete, product_merge: <merge commit>, catalog regenerated, check run, git pull --rebase, push.

  7. If step 6 fails after the product merged, retry the pull, rebase and push. Never revert the product merge. The phase stays active until the completion commit lands.

A repository with no origin, or whose origin is a path on this machine (tests, local-only use), is merged locally instead: git merge --no-ff into dev, then push if a remote exists. product.py merge-route decides from the origin URL. A hosted origin always takes the pull request: if gh cannot reach it, session-close stops and reports instead of merging locally.

Two repositories: control and product

Source plugins/idea-realization/docs/two-repositories.md, up to “A merged phase without its completion record”

A team that builds a product with this pipeline keeps two repositories.

  • The control repository holds every governed record and every rule: ideas, requirements, plans, decisions, the backlog, session records, review records, agents, skills and this plugin. It is where work is decided, claimed and recorded. Every developer clones it from one shared remote.
  • The product repository holds the product: its code, its tests and its CI. It carries as little process as possible.

Agent sessions start in the control repository, so its agents, skills and instruction files (CLAUDE.md, and AGENTS.md where it has one) apply, and reach the product worktree with --add-dir (or /add-dir inside a session).

Naming the product repository

.idea-realization/product.yaml is tracked in the control repository and says what is the same on every machine:

schema_version: 1
name: <product name>
integration_branch: dev
ci_workflow: product-ci.yml   # none only for a product with no CI

What differs per machine, or must not be tracked, is configured in each machine's untracked .idea-realization/local.yaml (copy local.example.yaml; it is read from the primary checkout), or with the environment variable, which takes precedence:

KeyEnvironment variableMeaning
product_rootIDEA_REALIZATION_PRODUCT_ROOTThis machine's product checkout; outside the control repository
product_worktree_dirIDEA_REALIZATION_PRODUCT_WORKTREE_DIRWhere product worktrees go; default ../<product>-worktrees, beside the product checkout
product_remoteIDEA_REALIZATION_PRODUCT_REMOTEGit URL of the product repository
product_githubIDEA_REALIZATION_PRODUCT_GITHUBThe product repository on GitHub, as <org>/<repo>
control_remoteIDEA_REALIZATION_CONTROL_REMOTEGit URL of the control repository
control_githubIDEA_REALIZATION_CONTROL_GITHUBThe control repository on GitHub, as <org>/<repo>

The repository URLs live in local.yaml because a URL can name an organization that must not appear in a tracked file. A team whose URLs may be tracked can set remote and github in product.yaml, and control.remote and control.github in project.yaml, instead; a value in local.yaml or the environment still overrides them. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/paths.py show prints each value and the file or variable it came from.

uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/product.py verify prints the product checkout, its integration branch and its worktree directory, and refuses unless the checkout's origin is the resolved product_remote. While product_remote is not set it refuses and says to set it in local.yaml. Every procedure that acts on the product repository runs it first, so a wrong path cannot send work into the wrong repository.

Without product_root, everything that only reads or writes the control repository still works: ideas, plans, the backlog, the checks. Anything that needs the product checkout says it is not configured and stops.

Branches

Both repositories have the same branches and names.

BranchHoldsHow work reaches it
mainreleased worka pull request from dev, merged with a merge commit, per release
devthe integration branch (integration_branch in product.yaml and in the control repository's configuration)feature branches through a pull request merged with a merge commit; in the control repository, bookkeeping commits directly
agent/<phase-id>one claimed phase; the same name in both repositoriescut from origin/dev, merged by session-close
agent/<handle>-<slug>owner-directed work with no phasecut from origin/dev, merged the same way

Bookkeeping commits go directly onto control dev, never through a pull request: claim commits, completion commits, idea commits and workstream claims. Pull origin dev before any work, and push a bookkeeping commit as soon as it is made, so peers see it.

Where each step happens

StepRepositoryWhere
Ideas, triage, partition, plans, requirements, decisionscontrolas usual
The backlog, the claim commit, the catalogcontrolprimary checkout, control integration branch, pushed at once
The phase's code, tests and verification commandsproductagent/<phase-id> in <product worktree dir>/<phase-id>
The session record, checkpoints, review verdict recordscontrolthe paired agent/<phase-id> in <worktree dir>/<phase-id>
The gating reviewbothjudges the product diff against the control documents
The control mergecontrolpull request from agent/<phase-id> into the integration branch, merged with a merge commit
The product mergeproductpull request from agent/<phase-id>, merged with a merge commit after the required check passes; its second parent must be the reviewed commit
The completion recordcontrolone commit directly on the control integration branch, after the product merge, pushed at once

The session-start and session-close skills carry out these steps in order. A repository with no origin, or whose origin is a path on this machine, makes the same merges locally with git merge --no-ff (product.py merge-route decides); a hosted one whose gh fails stops instead.

Paths in a phase

A path with the prefix product: is a path in the product repository; a path without one is a path in the control repository. The prefix is used in a phase's deliverables and completion_evidence, and in a system's paths in systems.yaml:

deliverables:
  - product:src/api/
  - product:test/test_api.py
  - docs/decisions/<code>-api-shape.md
verification:
  - uv run pytest
  - "control: uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py"
  • The concurrency check compares declared paths as written, so two phases that both declare product:src/api/ collide, and product:src/ and src/ do not.
  • A product: completion evidence file is checked in the product checkout when this machine has one; without one, only its shape is checked. For a phase that names its product_merge, the file is read at that commit, not in the working tree, so a checkout that has not pulled the merge still finds it. When the checkout does not hold the commit, the check prints a cannot tell note: fetch the product checkout and run the check again.
  • A verification command runs in the product worktree unless it starts with control:.

Approval

A passing gating review approves the product merge and the control merge that carries the phase's records. There is no separate per-merge approval. The owner keeps every decision the backlog protocol reserves, such as accepting plans and ranking the queue.

Branching and CI (OPS-001)

Source docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, from “7. CI: the control repository”

7. CI: the control repository

Workflow: .github/workflows/control-ci.yml. One job, verify.

Triggers: every pull request to dev or main, and every push to dev, main or agent/**. Runs are grouped per ref; a new push cancels the run still in progress for the same ref.

Steps, in order:

StepCommand
Installastral-sh/setup-uv with Python 3.12, cache keyed on uv.lock; uv sync --locked --extra dev
Lintuv run ruff check tools/ test/
Doctoruv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/doctor.py
Product repository settingsfails without PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN or a product slug; reads the product integration branch from .idea-realization/product.yaml
Product checkoutactions/checkout of the product repository with PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN, fetch-depth: 0, moved to $RUNNER_TEMP/product
Repository checkproduct.py verify, then check.py, with IDEA_REALIZATION_REQUIRE_PRODUCT=1
Folder testsuv run pytest -q test
Plugin testsuv run pytest -q, from plugins/idea-realization/
Private-content checkuv run python tools/check_confidential.py with the deny-list

Doctor and check run with IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$GITHUB_WORKSPACE, so the scripts resolve this checkout. The test steps run without it: the plugin tests build temporary repositories and fail when that variable points them at the checkout.

The repository check verifies product merges against the product repository itself. CI checks the product repository out read-only (full history, all branches, credentials not kept in its git config), moves it to $RUNNER_TEMP/product because product_root must be outside the control checkout, and runs the check with IDEA_REALIZATION_PRODUCT_ROOT and IDEA_REALIZATION_PRODUCT_REMOTE (https://github.com/<org>/<repo>, the origin actions/checkout sets) pointing at it. product.py verify runs first, so a checkout whose origin does not match fails the step. IDEA_REALIZATION_REQUIRE_PRODUCT=1 makes the reviews check fail when no product checkout is configured, and makes a cannot tell about whether a product_merge landed an error instead of a note, so CI never passes a completion it did not check: a made-up product_merge fails as stranded, and a merge commit whose second parent was not reviewed fails. In that one step the token is also given to git as an HTTP header for the reviews check's git ls-remote of the product's origin.

There is no scaffold step. A fresh checkout has no .idea-realization/staging/ directory, because it is gitignored; doctor reports it as absent and does not fail on it. Running the scaffold in CI would also rewrite the tracked .idea-realization/install-state.json.

The deny-list comes from the repository secret DENY_LIST, one identifier per line. The workflow masks each entry in the log, writes the list to $RUNNER_TEMP, passes its path in PRIVATE_DENY_LIST, and deletes it after the check. A missing secret fails the run, in this repository and in the product repository alike: a run that could not look for the identifiers has not shown that none are present. A pull request from a fork gets no secrets, so its run fails too. The owner sets the secret once in each repository:

gh secret set DENY_LIST --repo <org>/<control-repo> < .private/deny-list.txt
gh secret set DENY_LIST --repo <org>/<product-repo> < .private/deny-list.txt

The product checkout needs the repository secret PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN and the product's name on GitHub. A missing token fails the run, as a missing DENY_LIST does: a run that could not read the product repository has not shown that the recorded merges are real. A pull request from a fork gets no secrets, so its run fails at this step too.

  • The token. A fine-grained personal access token, or a GitHub App installation token, that can read the product repository and nothing else:

    • resource owner: the organization (or user) that owns the product repository; an organization that requires approval of fine-grained tokens holds it as pending until an administrator approves it;
    • repository access: Only select repositories, with the product repository as the only one;
    • repository permissions: Contents: Read-only. GitHub adds Metadata: Read-only itself as mandatory. Grant nothing else: no write permission, no other repository, no account or organization permission;
    • expiration: a date, at most 366 days ahead (an organization policy can set a shorter maximum). For a GitHub App the same holds: installed on the product repository only, with Contents read-only and Metadata read-only.

  • Who creates and rotates it. The repository owner. Before the token expires, the owner creates a new one with the same settings, replaces the secret, and deletes the old token. An expired token fails the Check out the product repository step (docs/guides/OPS-008-troubleshooting.md).

  • Where it is set. As a GitHub Actions secret on the control repository, never in a file:

    gh secret set PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN --repo <org>/<control-repo>

    gh prompts for the value, so it is not left in the shell history.

  • The product's name. The repository variable PRODUCT_GITHUB on the control repository, as <org>/<repo>: gh variable set PRODUCT_GITHUB --repo <org>/<control-repo> --body <org>/<repo>. When it is unset the workflow uses product_github as paths.py resolves it, which in CI is the github: field of .idea-realization/product.yaml. A team whose organization name must not be tracked uses the variable. Neither set fails the run.

The control job is not a required check: bookkeeping commits go to dev directly and must not wait for CI. A red run on dev or main is an alarm; fix it forward with a new commit.

8. CI: the product repository

The product workflow, .github/workflows/product-ci.yml, ships in the product-repository template (templates/product-repo/). Its job is also named verify, and it never deploys or calls AWS or Bedrock. The rulesets require a check named exactly verify reported by GitHub Actions, so the job must keep that id and must not set a different name:.

9. Rulesets

Branch and tag protection is defined as GitHub repository rulesets in .github/rulesets/:

FileRepositoryProtectsRules
control-dev.jsoncontroldevblock force-push and deletion; no pull request requirement (bookkeeping is direct)
control-main.jsoncontrolmainblock force-push and deletion; restrict updates (only the main merger); pull request required, 0 approvals, merge commit only
product-dev.jsonproductdevblock force-push and deletion; pull request required, 0 approvals, merge commit only; required check verify
product-main.jsonproductmainsame as product-dev.json, plus restrict updates (only the main merger)
demo-tags-create.jsonbothtags demo-*restrict creations (only the main merger)
demo-tags-protect.jsonbothtags demo-*block deletion, update and force-push; no bypass actor

No ruleset requires linear history, because merges are merge commits. The bypass list is empty in every ruleset file; the apply script adds the main merger to the two *-main.json rulesets and to demo-tags-create.json when it applies them, and nothing else has a bypass actor. The required check does not require the branch to be up to date with dev (strict_required_status_checks_policy: false): updating the branch would change its head and break --match-head-commit <reviewed_commit>. Session-close rebases onto origin/dev before the review instead.

Repository settings applied with the rulesets: default branch dev; merge commits allowed; squash and rebase merges switched off.

The owner applies them. Nothing runs this automatically. Push both dev and main to the new repository first, then:

tools/github/apply_rulesets.sh <org>/<control-repo> control user:<owner-login>
tools/github/apply_rulesets.sh <org>/<product-repo> product user:<owner-login>

The third argument names who may merge into main (below). Use the same value for both repositories.

Before it calls GitHub, the script checks that <org>/<repo> is the repository this machine's .idea-realization/local.yaml names for that kind: control_github for control, product_github for product (or, when those are unset, the GitHub repository in control_remote or product_remote). It refuses when the value is unset or differs, so the control rulesets cannot be applied to the product repository or the reverse.

It then checks that the main merger (the third argument) already has access to that repository, and refuses before it changes any setting or sends any ruleset when it does not. For user:<login> it calls gh api repos/<org>/<repo>/collaborators/<login>, which GitHub answers with 204 for a collaborator (outside collaborators, organization members with direct, team or base-permission access, and organization owners) and 404 otherwise. For team:<org>/<team-slug> it calls gh api orgs/<org>/teams/<team-slug>/repos/<org>/<repo>, which answers 204 when the team has access and 404 when it does not. This stops a mistyped login, or the wrong team, from being given the bypass on main and on demo-* tag creation.

The script needs gh signed in as an administrator of the repository. It is safe to run again: a ruleset whose name already exists on the repository is updated in place, otherwise it is created. It prints each action it took.

Plan requirement: rulesets on a private repository need a paid GitHub plan for the organization. Both repositories live in the owner's work organization, and its plan applies.

Who merges to main

Only the owner merges dev into main, in both repositories, and GitHub enforces it:

  • Both *-main.json rulesets carry the update rule (shown as "Restrict updates" in GitHub's settings): only an actor on the ruleset's bypass list may change main at all, and merging a pull request into main is such a change.
  • The apply script puts exactly one actor on that bypass list, the main merger, with bypass mode pull_request. The main merger can merge a pull request into main but cannot push to it directly; the pull request rule still applies to them. Everyone else, including other administrators acting through a pull request, is refused.
  • As committed, the bypass list is empty, so applying a *-main.json file by hand (without the script) leaves main closed to everyone until the script is run.

The actor is given as the script's third argument and its numeric id is looked up on GitHub when the script runs. No account or team name is written into this repository.

What the owner sets up, once:

  1. Choose the main merger. The direct form is your own account: user:<owner-login>. GitHub has accepted individual users as bypass actors on repository rulesets since May 2026 (actor type User). If the organization's policy does not allow a user bypass, create a team in the organization whose only member is you, give it at least write access to both repositories, and pass team:<org>/<team-slug> instead. Keep that team to one member: everyone in it can merge to main.

  2. Push dev and main to both repositories, then run the two commands above with that argument.

  3. Confirm the result:

    gh api repos/<org>/<control-repo>/rulesets --jq '.[] | "\(.id) \(.name)"'
gh api repos/<org>/<control-repo>/rulesets/<id of control-main> --jq '.bypass_actors'

    The second command must print one actor, with bypass_mode pull_request.

  4. If the main merger changes, re-run the script with the new argument. It replaces the bypass list.

What this does not stop: an organization owner or repository administrator can edit or delete the ruleset itself. That is a GitHub limit; keep the administrator role to the owner.

Who creates demo-* tags

Only the main merger (the owner) creates demo-* tags, in both repositories, and nobody can move or delete one:

  • demo-tags-create.json carries the creation rule ("Restrict creations") on refs/tags/demo-*. The apply script puts the main merger on its bypass list with bypass mode always. GitHub accepts bypass mode pull_request only on branch rulesets, and a tag is pushed, not merged, so always is the mode that lets the owner push a new tag. Everyone else's tag push is refused.
  • demo-tags-protect.json carries the deletion, update and non_fast_forward rules on the same tags and has no bypass actor, so the owner cannot move or delete a tag either.
  • They are two rulesets because a bypass actor bypasses every rule in its ruleset; GitHub has no per-rule bypass. One ruleset with the owner on its bypass list would let the owner move and delete demo-* tags.
  • As committed, the bypass list of demo-tags-create.json is empty, so applying it by hand (without the script) leaves demo-* tag creation closed to everyone until the script is run.

To confirm, after the script has run: the bypass list of demo-tags-create prints one actor with bypass_mode always, and that of demo-tags-protect prints []:

gh api repos/<org>/<control-repo>/rulesets/<id of demo-tags-create> --jq '.bypass_actors'
gh api repos/<org>/<control-repo>/rulesets/<id of demo-tags-protect> --jq '.bypass_actors'

A repository the earlier version of the script was applied to also has a ruleset named demo-tags (deletion, update and force-push protection, no bypass actor). The script matches rulesets by name, so it does not update or remove it. It protects the same tags the same way as demo-tags-protect and does no harm; the owner may delete it in the repository's ruleset settings.

The review gate

A passing gating review is the approval to merge a phase. This chapter covers who reviews, what the reviewer is given, and how a verdict is recorded.

Validating mode (OPS-004)

Source docs/guides/OPS-004-validating-mode.md, from “Phase reviews” up to “Infrastructure and spend”

Phase reviews

The gating review

The session-close skill runs it (step 3) after rebasing both branches and running the verification. Its brief to the reviewer contains:

  • the phase id with its scope, acceptance, verification and deliverables pasted in;
  • the product worktree path and the range origin/dev...HEAD, and the control worktree path and the same range there, for the reviewer to diff and log itself;
  • the paths of the phase's requirement and plan;
  • the verification output, as evidence it may re-run but must not take on trust.

phase-adversary replies with a first line VERDICT: pass or VERDICT: reject, the phase id and the reviewed commit, then a judgement per acceptance condition, then ranked findings. The session records it with gating: true (the schema's verdict values are pass and reject). A passing gating verdict is the approval for merging both the product and the control pull requests. Two rejects in a row on the same finding: the phase stays active and goes to the owner.

The shadow judge: review-judge

review-judge judges the same diff without a shell. It has no tool that runs a command, so its brief must carry everything: the phase's scope, acceptance and verification, the commit range and its diff, and evidence files holding the captured output of each verification command and gate check, each with its command and exit code. It is briefed by the session running the review, never by the session that built the phase.

Its verdict is recorded with gating: false and decides nothing. It runs in shadow until the owner decides whether to promote it, by comparing its verdicts with the gating reviewer's.

What exists today: the session-close skill's text names only the gating reviewer. Dispatching review-judge and writing its evidence files is a step the reviewing session does by hand, after the gating review's verification run, against the same reviewed_commit. This repository has no script that writes the evidence files.

Mechanical gates: validator-check

Dispatch it with an absolute worktree path and the exact checklist, usually:

  • IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=<control worktree> uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py;
  • uv run python tools/check_confidential.py, with the changes staged first, because it reads git ls-files;
  • the test commands, and the product's own test and lint commands for the product worktree;
  • drift checks such as a regenerated catalog that must diff clean.

It reports each gate's real result, with failures verbatim.

Team workflow (OPS-005)

Source docs/guides/OPS-005-team-workflow.md, from “4. Review and merge” up to “5. Daily cadence”

4. Review and merge

The session-close skill carries this sequence; OPS-001 has the git and GitHub commands.

  1. Run the phase's verification. Rebase both feature branches onto origin/dev and re-run the check and the product's tests.
  2. The gating review (phase-adversary) judges the product diff against the phase's control documents. Every finding is fixed or explicitly accepted; a fix is re-reviewed. session-close does not run the shadow review-judge; another session may (OPS-004, "The shadow judge").
  3. A passing gating review is the approval to merge both the product branch and the control branch. There is no separate per-merge approval.
  4. The session pushes both feature branches and opens a pull request to dev in each repository. It merges each with a merge commit (never squash or rebase merge), pinned to the commit that was reviewed so GitHub refuses the merge if the branch moved after the review. The product pull request waits for its required check verify first.
  5. The completion commit goes directly to control dev: the phase's status: complete, the product merge commit, the regenerated catalog. git pull --rebase, then push.

If the completion push fails after the product merged, retry the pull, rebase and push. Never revert the product merge. Until the completion commit lands, the phase stays active (plugins/idea-realization/docs/two-repositories.md, "A merged phase without its completion record").

Validating mode (OPS-004)

Source docs/guides/OPS-004-validating-mode.md, from “Reviewing a peer's ready branch”

Reviewing a peer's ready branch

What exists today: there is no review skill. The gating review is run by the session-close skill inside the session that holds the phase, and it is that session that records the gating verdict and merges. A second developer can still review a peer's pushed branch by hand, with the same agents. Such a review does not replace the gating review in the peer's session-close.

  1. In each primary checkout, git fetch origin and confirm the peer has pushed agent/<phase-id>. If not, ask them to push it; pushing their own branch needs no approval.

  2. Create a detached review worktree in each repository, outside the repository, at the pushed commit, so nothing you do moves the peer's branch:

    git -C <product checkout> worktree add --detach <product worktree dir>/review-<phase-id> origin/agent/<phase-id>
git worktree add --detach <worktree dir>/review-<phase-id> origin/agent/<phase-id>

    Install the product worktree's own environment there; never link the peer's.

  3. Note the product commit you will review: git -C <product review worktree> rev-parse HEAD.

  4. Dispatch a fresh phase-adversary (or validator-code) with the brief session-close step 3 describes: the phase's scope, acceptance, verification and deliverables from the backlog on control dev, both review worktree paths with the range origin/dev...HEAD, and the requirement and plan paths. Give it no explanation from the peer.

  5. Send the peer the full reply, with the reviewed commit, so they can fix or accept each finding. Do not commit a verdict record on the peer's branch: their branch, their records.

  6. Remove both review worktrees from the primary checkouts with git worktree remove.

Whether a peer's review may stand as the gating review, and how it would be recorded, is not settled; until the owner decides, the gating verdict is the one session-close records.

Bookkeeping

The commits that go directly on control dev (ideas, claims, completion records and workstream claims) and the rules for plans, phases and the catalog.

Branching and CI (OPS-001)

Source docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, from “3. What goes direct to control dev” up to “4. Merging a phase: pull request with a merge commit”

3. What goes direct to control dev

Control bookkeeping is committed directly on control dev and pushed, with no pull request:

  • claim commits (session-start),
  • completion commits (session-close: status: complete, product_merge, regenerated catalog),
  • idea commits,
  • workstream claims,
  • a developer's own entry in docs/systems.yaml (ONBOARDING.md, section 3, step 5).

If the push is rejected because someone else pushed first: git pull --rebase origin dev, run the repository check again, then push. Never force-push.

Everything else, in both repositories, reaches dev through a pull request.

On control dev this is a rule you follow, not a rule GitHub enforces. Control dev has no pull request requirement, because bookkeeping commits go there directly, so GitHub would accept a feature branch pushed or merged straight to it. Do not do that: a control feature branch goes through a pull request like a product one. Product dev does enforce it.

CLAUDE.md

Source CLAUDE.md, from “Plans: governed and ephemeral” up to “Concurrent agents: claim a phase”

Plans: governed and ephemeral

  • A governed plan is a document under docs/plans/ with a code and front matter, approved by the owner, and decomposed into backlog phases. It is the only kind of plan work is claimed from.
  • An ephemeral working plan — a scratch list for one session — lives under _working/, which is gitignored and ungoverned. Nothing claims work from it, and nothing there is deleted without the owner's approval.

Documentation governance

  • Follow plugins/idea-realization/docs/protocol.md for document front matter and lifecycle, and plugins/idea-realization/docs/document-codes.md for codes.
  • Name each document <code>-<slug>.md, in a folder its series allows (docs/codes.yaml).
  • Regenerate docs/catalog.md after changing any document (catalog skill); the check fails while it is stale.
  • Update docs/systems.yaml when a component's responsibilities change.
  • Plans describe proposed work; verify the code before claiming a capability exists.

Session backlog

  • Capture every approved plan's phases in backlog/backlog.yaml before implementing its work.
  • Each phase is one session: one concrete outcome, with acceptance checks and its declared systems and deliverables.
  • Up to max_active phases run at once (backlog/backlog.yaml).
  • Remove a phase from next_up in the same change that completes it.
  • Keep deferred work visible with a resume condition; split a phase that exceeds one session.
  • Checkpoint progress with the checkpoint skill as often as useful. It never marks a phase complete; only session-close does, after its gating review.
  • New asks that arise mid-session are recorded as ideas at once (idea skill), not folded into the current work.

Team workflow (OPS-005)

Source docs/guides/OPS-005-team-workflow.md, from “3. Claims” up to “4. Review and merge”

3. Claims

A phase is claimed on control dev, which holds the backlog (backlog/backlog.yaml), the lock table every developer reads. The session-start skill carries these steps; this is what it does and why.

  1. Pull first. In the primary checkout, git pull --rebase origin dev before any work. A claim made against a stale backlog is checked against stale claims.
  2. One phase per agent. An agent id is <handle>/agent-<name>, for example ana/agent-builder; the backlog schema requires the agent- prefix. Each agent holds at most one active phase. One developer may run several agents, each with its own phase.
  3. The active-claim limit is max_active: 15 across the whole team. The check refuses a claim past it; a refusal means choosing other work, never waiting.
  4. The check decides whether a claim is safe. It refuses a phase whose systems, deliverables or dependency chain overlap an active phase, or whose deliverables fall inside a workstream another developer owns.
  5. Claim directly on control dev and push immediately. The claim commit changes only the phase's status: active and agent, the backlog's updated, and the regenerated catalog.
  6. A rejected push means a peer claimed between your check and your push. Run git pull --rebase, re-run the check, and confirm the claim is still safe before pushing again. If the check now refuses it, release it and choose another phase.

Then the work happens on agent/<phase-id> branches cut from origin/dev in both repositories, each in its own worktree (CLAUDE.md, "work in a worktree").

Assignment

The owner assigns a phase to a developer by setting owner: <handle> on that phase in the backlog. Anyone may still claim it: the check warns when the claimant is not the phase's owner and never refuses. Treat the warning as a question to ask the assigned developer before going further.

CLAUDE.md

Source CLAUDE.md, from “Concurrent agents: complete and hand off” up to “Concurrent agents: resolve collisions”

Concurrent agents: complete and hand off

Perform these in order. session-close carries out steps 4 to 9; the git and GitHub commands are in OPS-001, section 4.

  1. Run every command in the phase's verification list in the worktree it belongs to and keep the real output. A failing check is a result, not a reason to skip the step.
  2. Write the session record (kind: session) with its code from next-code, on the control branch.
  3. Confirm each acceptance condition. If one does not hold, leave the phase active or return it to queued with an exact next_action, releasing your claim.
