  4. Rebase both branches onto origin/<integration branch> and re-run the verification, the repository check and the product's tests. Never merge a red rebase.
  5. Run the gating review (phase-adversary); the verdicts are recorded under docs/reviews/. review-judge is optional: it runs in shadow only when another session dispatches it (OPS-004); session-close does not. Fix or explicitly accept every finding, and re-review after a fix.
  6. Confirm both primary checkouts are clean. Never stash or overwrite a peer's uncommitted work.
  7. Merge, on a passing verdict only: a pull request to dev in each repository, control first, then product after verify passes, each with a merge commit pinned to the reviewed head. The product merge commit's second parent must be the verdict's reviewed_commit; if it is not, stop and report it.
  8. Record completion in one commit directly on control dev: status, session, completion_evidence, product_merge, and the regenerated catalog. If the push fails after the product merged, retry; never revert the product merge. The phase stays active until it lands.
  9. Remove your worktrees and branches once their content has merged.

If a head moved after the review or the branch conflicts with the trunk, rebase again and re-run the checks and the review; never merge an unreviewed head.

Two repositories: control and product

Source plugins/idea-realization/docs/two-repositories.md, from “A merged phase without its completion record”

A merged phase without its completion record

session-close merges the product pull request before it writes the completion record, so the one state a failed close can leave behind is product code merged on the product integration branch while the control repository still records the phase active. Nothing is wrong with the merged code: it passed the gating review, which is the approval.

Recover it by landing the completion commit, never by undoing the merge:

  1. In the control primary checkout, git pull --rebase, regenerate the catalog, run the check, and git push. Repeat until the push lands. A backlog conflict keeps both sides.
  2. The completion commit names the merge commit as product_merge. Read it from the pull request (gh pr view <n> --json mergeCommit) if the session that merged it has ended.
  3. Never revert the product merge to make the two repositories agree. Until the completion commit lands, the phase stays active and its claim stays held.

A stranded phase

The reverse state is a phase recorded complete whose product_merge is not on the product integration branch. session-close does not produce it, because it records completion only after the merge landed; it means the completion record was written by hand, or the product integration branch lost the commit. The check reports it as stranded wherever a product checkout is configured.

A product checkout that has not fetched does not know a peer's merge, so before reporting stranded the check asks origin where the integration branch is now (git ls-remote, which changes nothing). It reports stranded only when this checkout already holds origin's tip and the commit is not in its history. When origin cannot be read, or has commits this checkout has not fetched, it prints cannot tell whether product_merge … landed instead, which is not an error.

  1. Fetch the product checkout and run the check again (git -C <product checkout> fetch origin). A cannot tell note, or a stranded line that goes away after the fetch, means the checkout was behind: the phase is complete and nothing else is done. Never reopen a phase on a cannot tell note.
  2. Only if stranded remains after the fetch: confirm it on the forge, which is the record of what merged (gh pr view <n> --json state,mergeCommit in the product checkout, where <n> is the phase's product pull request). If the pull request merged as product_merge, the product integration branch lost the commit; stop and report it to the owner rather than reopening. If the forge does not answer — gh pr view fails, no pull request number is recorded for the phase, or its state does not show whether it merged as product_merge — that is also cannot tell: stop, report it to the owner, and do not reopen the phase.
  3. Only when the forge shows the pull request did not merge as product_merge, reopen the phase in the control repository: set it back to active with a next_action naming the stranded merge, and remove its product_merge, in one commit directly on the control integration branch. Then rebase the product branch, run the verification, review the new HEAD, and close the session again.

Control CI checks for real: it checks the product repository out with a read-only token and runs the check with IDEA_REALIZATION_REQUIRE_PRODUCT=1, under which a missing product checkout is an error and a cannot tell about landing is an error instead of a note. So in CI a product_merge that does not exist, is not on the integration branch, or is a merge commit whose second parent was not reviewed fails the run (the branching and CI guide, section 7).

Without any product checkout on a developer's machine (product_root unset) and without that requirement, the check cannot test landing at all. It still fails a complete phase whose control records do not agree: no passing gating verdict for that phase on the product repository, or a product_merge or reviewed_commit that is not a full commit id. A product_merge equal to the reviewed commit (a fast-forward) passes. Any other product_merge can only be a merge commit whose second parent was reviewed, which needs the product repository to read, so the check prints product_merge … not checked: no product checkout is configured for that phase instead of an error.

Never edit product_merge to a commit the recorded verdict did not judge: it is the commit the verdict judged (a fast-forward) or a merge commit whose second parent is that commit.

Team workflow (OPS-005)

Source docs/guides/OPS-005-team-workflow.md, from “5. Daily cadence” up to “7. Release”

5. Daily cadence

WhenWhat
Morning, 15 minutesSync: everyone pulls dev in both repositories. Render the backlog; the owner ranks next_up and assigns phases (owner: <handle>); each developer's agents claim. Name any interface that is about to change.
MiddayIntegrate: rebase every open feature branch onto origin/dev in both repositories and re-run the check and tests, so conflicts surface while they are small. Merge whatever has passed its gating review.
End of dayEach phase is either closed through session-close or checkpointed with the checkpoint skill, so the next session can resume from the record. Record what the day decided or learned in the brain (brain.py new <kind>, committed with brain/index.md on the phase's control branch before session-close, or on an agent/<handle>-<slug> branch through a pull request). Push every feature branch, so no work exists only on one machine. The owner reviews the day's ideas.

Ideas raised during the day are recorded with the idea skill, not folded into the phase in progress.

6. Conflicts

  • backlog/backlog.yaml conflicts are normal: two developers edited different phases in one file. Keep both sides: the peer's phases verbatim and your own phase's edits, with updated set to today. Never resolve it with --ours or --theirs; either one deletes a peer's work.
  • A duplicate document code means two allocations on separate machines took the same code before either merged. Codes carry the allocating developer's handle (PLAN-<handle>-NNN), so this happens only for a governance code, for two sub-codes under one plan, or for one developer allocating on two machines. Whoever integrates second renumbers: allocate a new code, rename the file and update every reference (backlog-protocol.md, section 12).
  • A source conflict between two phases declared disjoint means a declaration is wrong. Stop, do not force the merge, and fix the declarations before either phase completes; record the choice in the decision record.
  • Never revert a peer's commit. A branch that goes red after a rebase means a peer changed something it depended on: fix your branch against the current dev.

Workstreams: who owns which paths

Source plugins/idea-realization/docs/workstreams.md, whole document

A team of developers on separate machines works in two layers.

  • The inner layer is the phase claim: one phase at a time per agent, claimed on the control integration branch, with the concurrency check refusing phases whose systems, deliverables or dependencies overlap. It works the same for one developer running one agent as for one running several.
  • The outer layer is the workstream: a part of the product one developer owns, such as the user interface, the product's own agent orchestration or the backend. A workstream names the paths it covers. Other developers' phases stay out of them.

A workstream is ownership, not a lock. It is claimed once and held, so the git race that a frequent claim would run into almost never happens. It feeds the phase claim rather than replacing it: the check refuses a phase whose deliverables fall inside a workstream someone else owns.

The registry

docs/workstreams.yaml, validated by .idea-realization/schemas/workstreams.schema.json:

schema_version: 1
workstreams:
  - id: ui
    title: User interface
    owner: ""            # a developer handle once claimed
    status: open         # open | claimed
    paths:
      - product:web/
    interfaces: []       # documents stating what this workstream provides to others

The owner writes the list of workstreams. Developers claim them.

Developers and handles

A developer is an entry in the owners map of docs/systems.yaml that lists their git author emails:

owners:
  repository-owner: The person accountable for this repository.
  ana:
    description: Ana, user interface.
    emails: [ana@example.com]

The key is the developer's handle: lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter, at most sixteen characters. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/identity.py prints yours, from git config user.email. The handle scopes every identifier a developer allocates, so two developers working offline never allocate the same one:

  • an idea id is <handle>-NNNNNN, counting that developer's own ideas;
  • a document code in a scoped series is <SERIES>-<handle>-NNN or <SERIES>-<handle>-YYYY-MM-DD-NN (document-codes.md);
  • a phase id is phase-<track>-<handle>-<NN>; an id without a handle passes only when the backlog's legacy_phase_ids lists it (backlog-protocol.md);
  • a phase claim's agent is <handle>/agent-<name>.

Codes and phase ids carry the handle permanently, so a developer who leaves keeps their owners entry; removing it fails the check on every code and phase id that names them.

Claiming and releasing

uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py show
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py claim <id>
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/workstreams.py release <id>

claim writes your handle into an open workstream and validates the result; it never commits. Then, in the control repository's primary checkout on its integration branch:

  1. commit only docs/workstreams.yaml;
  2. push;
  3. if the push is rejected, someone else pushed first: git pull --rebase, then workstreams.py check. If the workstream is still yours and the check is clean, push again; if someone else claimed it, choose another. claim rewrites the whole file, so claims of two different workstreams can conflict in the rebase: keep both sides, each workstream keeping the lines its own claim wrote, and never resolve it with --ours or --theirs.

Only a workstream's owner releases it.

What the check enforces

workstreams.py check, which also runs as part of the plugin's check.py, reports:

  • two workstreams whose paths overlap;
  • a claimed workstream whose owner is not a developer, or an open one that names an owner;
  • once at least one workstream exists, an active or blocked phase whose agent carries no handle;
  • once at least one workstream exists, an active or blocked phase whose agent handle is not a developer (an owners key with emails), such as zed/agent-z when zed is not in owners;
  • an active or blocked phase whose deliverables fall inside a workstream claimed by another developer, unless the phase records that developer's approval:
cross_workstream:
  - workstream: ui
    approved_by: ana

A path outside every workstream is shared ground: only the phase claim applies to it.

Release and demo day

From dev to main, the demo-rc tags, the code freeze, and the runbook for the demo itself.

Branching and CI (OPS-001)

Source docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, from “5. Releases: dev to main, and demo tags” up to “7. CI: the control repository”

5. Releases: dev to main, and demo tags

For each demo release:

  1. The release developer (OPS-006, "Roles") opens a pull request from dev to main; the owner merges it with a merge commit. In the product repository the verify check must pass first. Only the owner can merge into main; GitHub refuses the merge for anyone else (section 9, "Who merges to main").

  2. The owner tags the merge on main with an annotated tag: demo-rc-<n>, counting up from 1. Only the owner can create demo-* tags; GitHub refuses the push for anyone else (section 9, "Who creates demo-* tags").

    git fetch origin
git tag -a demo-rc-3 origin/main -m "Demo release candidate 3"
git push origin demo-rc-3

  3. Tag the release that is shown on demo day demo-final as well.

Tag the control repository's main with the same name at the same time, so the two repositories can be matched to each other.

demo-* tags cannot be moved or deleted once pushed, by anyone, the owner included (the demo-tags-protect ruleset). If a tag is wrong, make a new release candidate with the next number.

Rollback: redeploy the previous demo-rc-<n> tag with the aws-deploy agent. Do not move or delete tags and do not rewrite main.

6. Code freeze and hotfixes

Code freeze is 2026-11-03 (demo day is 2026-11-05). After the freeze, only hotfix phases are built.

A hotfix is a normal phase: the fix is recorded as an idea, the owner registers a phase for it at the front of next_up, and it goes through the usual claim, gating review and pull request merge. It then goes to main in a new release pull request and gets the next demo-rc-<n> tag.

Team workflow (OPS-005)

Source docs/guides/OPS-005-team-workflow.md, from “7. Release”

7. Release

  • A demo release goes from dev to main through a pull request merged with a merge commit, in each repository.
  • Each release candidate gets an annotated tag on main: demo-rc-<n>. The one shown at the demo is also tagged demo-final.
  • Code freeze: 2026-11-03. After the freeze only fixes for the demo are merged, each as a phase through the same claim and gating review.
  • Release mechanics and tag protection are in OPS-001.

Demo day runbook (OPS-006)

Source docs/guides/OPS-006-demo-day-runbook.md, whole document

The steps from code freeze to the demo: release pull request, tags, local deployment, smoke test, rollback and the recorded fallback. The demo is on 2026-11-05; the code freeze is 2026-11-03. Both dates are also in .idea-realization/project.yaml (demo.date, demo.freeze).

Branching and CI rules are in the branching and CI guide (OPS-001). The AWS boundary is in aws/README.md. Neither is restated here.

Roles

Roles, not names. The owner assigns a person to each role before the freeze. Until the owner fills it in, the assignment is open:

RoleAssigned to
Release developernot yet assigned: the owner decides
Validatornot yet assigned: the owner decides
Sandbox administratornot yet assigned: the owner decides
Presenternot yet assigned: the owner decides

The owner records the handles here, or names the place the team uses instead.

RoleDoes
OwnerApproves each release pull request into main, creates the tags, chooses demo-final, decides on rollback. Only the owner merges into main and only the owner can push a demo-* tag; GitHub refuses both for anyone else.
Release developerOpens the release pull requests, runs the aws-deploy agent on their machine, keeps the deployment log.
ValidatorRuns the smoke test against each deployed release candidate and records the result.
Sandbox administratorThe person with administrator access to the sandbox account. Creates the permission boundary policy and service-linked roles, enables Bedrock model access, raises quotas. The deploy role cannot do any of these.
PresenterRuns the demo and decides on the day whether to switch to the recorded video.

One person may hold several roles. The release developer and the validator should be different people, so the smoke test is not run by the person who deployed.

Before the freeze (until 2026-11-03)

  1. Bedrock quota check. Dispatch the bedrock-claude-advisor agent with: "List the Anthropic models and inference profiles this account can call in its region, and the Bedrock service quotas for both models the product uses, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, through their US inference profiles (cross-region requests per minute and tokens per minute, one pair per model)." It reads them with tools/aws-sandbox read bedrock list-foundation-models, list-inference-profiles and service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code bedrock. Compare the quota with the load of the demo (presenter plus audience). If it is too low, the sandbox administrator requests an increase; quota increases can take days, so do this at least a week before the demo.
  2. Model access. If the advisor reports a model the account lists but cannot call, the sandbox administrator enables access. No agent can do this.
  3. Execution roles. The stacks create their roles under /app/ with the permission boundary, and the product CI's template check passes; any person-created role a stack imports exists under /app/ (aws/README.md, "What the deploy role can and cannot deploy").
  4. Smoke test written down. The validator writes the smoke test as a numbered list of checks with the expected result of each (URL, action, what must appear). Keep it in the product repository next to the deployment instructions. Which flows the demo shows is the owner's call.

Code freeze (2026-11-03)

After the freeze, only fixes reach dev, and each fix is a backlog phase:

  1. Record the problem as an idea (/idea-realization:idea).
  2. The owner registers a phase for it and puts it first in next_up.
  3. A developer claims it, builds it and closes it with session-close as usual. The gating review is never skipped.

A demo-day shortcut has been proposed (an agent/<handle>-hotfix-<slug> branch that skips the claim but not the review). It is not a ruling yet: ask the owner before using it.

Release candidate

Do this in both repositories (control and product), in the same order.

  1. Release pull request. From dev to main:

    gh pr create --base main --head dev --title "Release demo-rc-<n>" --body "<what changed since demo-rc-<n-1>>"

    In the product repository the required check verify must pass first: gh pr checks <number> --watch.

  2. Merge. The owner merges with a merge commit:

    gh pr merge <number> --merge

  3. Tag. The owner tags the merge commit on main with an annotated tag and pushes it. Only the owner can create a demo-* tag (the demo-tags-create ruleset, OPS-001 section 9); a tag pushed by anyone else is refused (OPS-008, "A push of a demo-* tag is refused").

    git fetch origin
git tag -a demo-rc-<n> origin/main -m "Demo release candidate <n>"
git push origin demo-rc-<n>

    <n> starts at 1 and increases by one per candidate. The two repositories carry the same demo-rc-<n> for the same release. Tags matching demo-* cannot be deleted or moved once the rulesets are applied, by anyone, the owner included, so check the commit before pushing the tag.

Local deployment

Deployment runs on the release developer's machine through the aws-deploy agent. There is no CI deployment (a draft plan for one is PLAN-002).

  1. Check the machine: uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe prints OK, and tools/aws-sandbox whoami prints both profiles and the read role's identity.

  2. Check out the tag in a separate product worktree, so no working branch is touched:

    git -C <product checkout> fetch --tags
git -C <product checkout> worktree add --detach <product worktree directory>/demo-rc-<n> demo-rc-<n>

  3. Dispatch aws-deploy with: the worktree path, the tag, the product's deploy command, and the smoke test's first check as the verification. The agent shows a diff or change set before it applies anything, and asks a person to approve every deletion.

  4. Keep its report (what was created or updated, and the verification output) in the session record or wherever the owner asks.

Smoke test

The validator runs the written smoke test against the deployed candidate and records, per check, pass or fail with the real output or a screenshot. Then dispatch aws-ops-inspector to read the deployed resources' state and recent errors. A failed check is a fix phase (see Code freeze), not a change made on the deployed stack.

Choosing demo-final

When a candidate has passed the smoke test, the owner tags the same commit demo-final in both repositories:

git tag -a demo-final demo-rc-<n>^{commit} -m "Demo final: demo-rc-<n>"
git push origin demo-final

demo-final is created once. If a later candidate replaces it before the demo, ask the owner: the demo-tags-protect ruleset blocks moving it, for the owner as well.

Rollback

Rollback is redeploying the previous candidate, never reverting commits on main:

  1. The owner decides to roll back and names the tag (demo-rc-<n-1>).
  2. The release developer checks out that tag in its own worktree (Local deployment, step 2) and dispatches aws-deploy with it.
  3. The validator runs the smoke test again.

A stack change that replaces or deletes a resource prompts for approval; say what will be deleted before approving. Data written by the newer version is not rolled back.

Recorded fallback video

  1. After the first candidate passes the smoke test, the presenter records the full demo flow against it. Record again after demo-final is chosen.
  2. Store the video outside both repositories (it is large, and may show account details). Ask the owner where.
  3. Check before recording that the screen shows no account id, credential, email address or other confidential identifier.
  4. The presenter switches to the video when the live demo fails and a rollback will not finish in time.

On the day (2026-11-05)

  1. One hour before: the validator runs the smoke test against the deployed demo-final.
  2. The release developer runs tools/aws-sandbox whoami on the deploying machine, so a rollback does not start with an expired login.
  3. The presenter has the video open and ready.
  4. No deployments except a rollback the owner orders.

After the demo

Run the teardown checklist in the cost guardrails guide (OPS-007).

AWS safety and cost guardrails

The sandbox's two roles and the machine rule are the boundary; the wrapper, the hook and the permission rules keep agents on the intended path. Spend is kept visible with a budget alarm, a daily review and tags.

CLAUDE.md

Source CLAUDE.md, from “AWS” up to “Running the checks”

AWS

  • The IAM roles and the machine rule are the boundary. The sandbox has a read-only role and a deploy role with no Organizations, account or billing permissions, which may change IAM only for the stack's own roles under /app/ that carry the permission boundary (aws/README.md). Each machine has one named profile for each, in untracked configuration.
  • Machine rule: a machine that runs agents holds no default or ambient AWS credentials — no default profile, no AWS_ credential or profile variables, no instance or container role — only the two named sandbox profiles. Then a command that gets past the hook finds no credentials but the sandbox roles. uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe checks it, and tools/aws-sandbox warns on every call when it finds a default profile or AWS_ variables.
  • Every AWS command goes through tools/aws-sandbox, which runs read and whoami with the read profile and write and exec with the deploy profile, and refuses a missing or default profile or one profile used for both. Never run the AWS CLI, an AWS SDK or a deployment tool any other way, never pass --profile or --region yourself, never set an AWS_ variable, and never read or change anything under ~/.aws/.
  • Reads (tools/aws-sandbox read ...) run freely, except the reads that reveal a secret.
  • Only the aws-deploy agent runs write or exec.
  • Deleting anything needs a person's approval each time; .claude/settings.json prompts for it. Say what will be deleted before the prompt appears. A refused prompt means stop.
  • A PreToolUse hook (tools/hooks/aws_guard.py) refuses AWS commands outside the wrapper, and write/exec from anyone but aws-deploy; the permission rules repeat the main refusals. Both match command text: they are guardrails, not the boundary. Never route around one, and report a rule that blocks legitimate work.

AWS sandbox setup

Source aws/README.md, whole document

How the team's sandbox account is set up so that agents can work in it safely. The IAM roles below, together with the machine rule, are the security boundary. The wrapper (tools/aws-sandbox), the PreToolUse hook (tools/hooks/aws_guard.py) and the permission rules in .claude/settings.json keep agents on the right path, but they match command text; what an agent can actually do is decided by the role its profile assumes.

The product this sandbox serves uses Step Functions; Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 5 for two agents, Claude Opus 5.5 for two) with Guardrails; Bedrock Knowledge Bases on an OpenSearch Serverless vector store; Textract; DynamoDB (one table set per tenant); S3 with one KMS key per tenant; KMS; a VPC with PrivateLink endpoints; Cognito; CloudTrail with its logs in an S3 Object Lock bucket; and a React examiner workbench on Amplify Hosting.

The machine rule

A machine that runs agents holds no default or ambient AWS credentials. No [default] or [profile default] section in ~/.aws/config or ~/.aws/credentials; no AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, AWS_PROFILE or container-credential variables in the environment; no EC2 instance role, container task role or other credentials the instance metadata service hands out. Only the two named sandbox profiles exist.

The AWS SDKs and CLI fall back to exactly those sources when no profile is named. With none of them present, a command that gets past the hook or the permission rules finds no credentials at all, or at most the deploy role, which cannot touch Organizations, account or billing, and can change IAM only for roles under /app/ that carry the permission boundary.

Check it on each machine, after setup and whenever its AWS configuration changes:

uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe

It reports each default profile, ambient variable and reachable metadata service, and with --probe asks AWS whom the default credential chain resolves to; it exits 1 if it finds anything. tools/aws-sandbox runs the file and environment checks on every call and prints what it finds as warnings.

The roles and policies

RoleUsed byPolicies
Readtools/aws-sandbox read and whoami; the agents aws-infra-reviewer, aws-ops-inspector, bedrock-claude-advisor, aws-cost-optimizerAWS managed ReadOnlyAccess, plus iam/read-only-guard-policy.json, plus (sandbox only) iam/read-sandbox-data-policy.json
Deploytools/aws-sandbox write and exec; the agent aws-deploy onlyiam/deploy-policy.json, plus iam/deploy-scope-policy.json
Application roles under /app/The product's own services at run time (Step Functions, Lambda, the Knowledge Base, Textract notifications, Cognito, CloudTrail, flow logs, Amplify)Whatever the stack grants, capped by the permission boundary iam/app-permissions-boundary.json

tools/aws-sandbox synth uses no role at all (see "Synthesizing without credentials").

  • read-only-guard-policy.json is a deny list added on top of ReadOnlyAccess: it refuses the reads that reveal a secret or a credential (secret values, parameter values and their history, login tokens, the environment variables of functions, Amplify apps and branches, CodeBuild projects and builds and ECS task definitions and tasks, Amplify basic-auth credentials and webhook URLs, Cognito app-client and identity-provider secrets; see "Reads the guard refuses" below), decrypting with KMS other than through S3 or DynamoDB, and the calls that cost money or run code (model invocation, agent and flow invocation, Knowledge Base retrieval, guardrail application, Textract analysis, Lambda invocation, assuming another role).
  • read-sandbox-data-policy.json lets the read role decrypt tenant data through S3 and DynamoDB and read Textract results (textract:Get*, List*), neither of which ReadOnlyAccess grants. The decrypt is limited three ways: to keys in the sandbox account (the key ARN pattern and aws:ResourceAccount), to keys with a tenant alias alias/<product>-tenant-* (kms:ResourceAliases), and to calls S3 or DynamoDB make on the role's behalf (kms:ViaService). See the warning below.
  • deploy-policy.json allows everything in the account except IAM, Organizations, account, billing, budget, cost and identity-center actions and assuming another role. Of IAM it allows: creating, changing and deleting roles under the path /app/ only when the role carries the permission boundary app-permissions-boundary (for CreateRole and PutRolePermissionsBoundary the condition key iam:PermissionsBoundary is the boundary in the request; for PutRolePolicy, AttachRolePolicy, DetachRolePolicy and DeleteRolePolicy it is the boundary already attached to the role, per the IAM page of the AWS Service Authorization Reference); passing /app/ roles to the product's services only (iam:PassedToService: Step Functions, Lambda, Bedrock, Textract, Cognito, CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, Amplify, EventBridge); reading /app/ roles; listing roles; and reading the boundary and AWS managed policies. Explicit Denies, which no Allow can override, refuse: any IAM change outside /app/ roles (users, groups, policies, service-linked roles, identity providers, the boundary policy itself); creating or changing an /app/ role without the boundary; removing a boundary; passing or reading any role outside /app/; the Organizations, account, billing and identity actions; stopping, deleting or updating the account's baseline CloudTrail trail; turning off Config or GuardDuty; bypassing S3 Object Lock governance retention; reading secret values; invoking a model through any inference profile other than a US geographic one (us.*); and any regional action outside the sandbox region, except the cross-region model routing of a US inference profile.
  • deploy-scope-policy.json limits the deploy role's changes to the product's own resources. It is a separate policy because deploy-policy.json is close to the 6,144-character limit for a managed policy. It denies creating, changing, publishing, invoking and deleting a Lambda function, a Step Functions state machine, a CloudFormation stack or a CodeBuild project whose name does not start with <product>-; changing, deploying to or deleting an Amplify app or branch that does not carry the tag project=<product>; adding or removing the project tag on any other Amplify resource; and starting an Amplify build job at all. <product> is the value that replaces REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCT_NAME. See "The deploy role changes only the product's own resources" below.
  • app-permissions-boundary.json caps every /app/ role at what the deploy role itself may do, minus secret reads, key policy changes and key deletion, Object Lock changes, turning off the audit trail, and assuming roles. It repeats every statement of deploy-scope-policy.json, so a role the stack creates cannot change another function, state machine, stack, build project or Amplify app either. A role the deploy role creates therefore never has more power than the deploy role. The boundary lets an application role pass /app/ roles to Textract and Bedrock (asynchronous Textract jobs and Bedrock jobs need it), and nothing else in IAM.
Reads the guard refuses, and what to read instead

The guard policy and the wrapper's SECRET_OPERATIONS refuse these reads, because their response carries a secret or a value that may be one (checked against the AWS API references, 2026-10-15):

Read (tools/aws-sandbox read ...)What the response carries
lambda get-function, get-function-configuration, list-functions, list-versions-by-functionThe function's environment variables (ListFunctions omits only the state fields)
amplify get-app, list-apps, get-branch, list-branchesEnvironment variables and basic-auth credentials of the app, its branches and its auto-branch settings
amplify get-webhook, list-webhooksThe webhook URL, which starts a build when called
codebuild batch-get-projects, batch-get-builds, batch-get-build-batchesBuild environment variables, including PLAINTEXT values
ecs describe-task-definition, describe-tasksContainer environment variables, and a task's environment overrides
cognito-idp describe-user-pool-clientThe app client secret
cognito-idp describe-identity-providerThe external provider's details, including its client_secret
ssm get-parameter-historyEach version's parameter value

Reviewers and aws-ops-inspector lose these reads. Use instead:

  • What is deployed: read cloudformation describe-stack-resources --stack-name <stack> (or list-stack-resources) for each function, state machine, Amplify app and branch and its physical id; read resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=project,Values=<product> for everything tagged.
  • How it is configured: the synthesized template (tools/aws-sandbox synth) or the deployed one (read cloudformation get-template), which hold runtime, memory, timeout, role and the environment variables as the stack wrote them; dynamic references stay unresolved there.
  • Lambda health: read lambda list-aliases, get-alias, get-function-concurrency, get-policy, list-event-source-mappings, the CloudWatch metrics (Errors, Throttles, Duration) and the function's log group.
  • Amplify deployments: read amplify list-jobs --app-id <id> --branch-name <branch> and get-job, with the app id from the stack resources; list-domain-associations.
  • CodeBuild and ECS, if the product ever uses them: read codebuild list-projects and list-builds-for-project; read ecs describe-services and list-tasks; and their logs.
  • Cognito: read cognito-idp list-user-pool-clients (ids and names) and describe-user-pool.

Kept, after checking: cloudformation describe-stacks and get-template (parameters marked NoEcho are masked in describe calls; a template holds what the repository holds, with dynamic references unresolved; a secret in Outputs or Metadata would show, which aws-infra-reviewer checks for); stepfunctions describe-state-machine (the definition, as in the repository); bedrock-agent get-knowledge-base and get-data-source (a Secrets Manager ARN, not the secret).

Revisit before real claimant data. The read role can decrypt tenant data and read Textract results because the sandbox holds synthetic data only (owner ruling, 2026-10-14). Before any real claimant document, name or identifier reaches this account, remove read-sandbox-data-policy.json from the read role and add kms:Decrypt back to the guard's unconditional deny. Agents would otherwise read personal data into their transcripts.

What the deploy role can and cannot deploy

The stack creates its own roles, under /app/ and with the boundary. The deploy role may create a role only when both hold: its path is /app/ (for example arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/app/ClaimsStack-StateMachineRole-1A2B3C) and its permission boundary is arn:aws:iam::<account>:policy/app-permissions-boundary. It may attach inline or AWS managed policies to such a role and delete it again. A role created without the path or the boundary fails with an access-denied error naming iam:CreateRole; fix the CDK app (below), not the policy.

The deploy role cannot create customer managed policies (AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy), users, groups, instance profiles or service-linked roles. CDK grants (table.grantReadWriteData(role)) produce inline policies (AWS::IAM::Policy), which are allowed on boundary roles.

CDK settings every product stack uses.

  1. CliCredentialsStackSynthesizer. The default CDK synthesizer assumes bootstrap roles, which sts:AssumeRole denies. With this synthesizer CDK deploys with the deploy profile's own credentials; an administrator bootstraps the account once.

  2. The permission boundary on every role, set once for the whole app. In cdk.json:

    { "context": { "@aws-cdk/core:permissionsBoundary": { "name": "app-permissions-boundary" } } }

    or in code, PermissionsBoundary.of(app).apply(ManagedPolicy.fromManagedPolicyName(app, 'AppBoundary', 'app-permissions-boundary')). Either applies the boundary to every Role in the app, including the roles that constructs create implicitly.

  3. The path /app/ on every role, and the boundary again on roles CDK writes as raw AWS::IAM::Role resources (custom-resource providers such as autoDeleteObjects, which the context setting has missed in some CDK versions). An aspect covers both:

    import { Aspects, CfnResource, IAspect, Stack } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { IConstruct } from 'constructs';

class AppRoles implements IAspect {
  visit(node: IConstruct): void {
    if (node instanceof CfnResource && node.cfnResourceType === 'AWS::IAM::Role') {
      node.addPropertyOverride('Path', '/app/');
      node.addPropertyOverride('PermissionsBoundary', Stack.of(node).formatArn({
        service: 'iam', region: '', resource: 'policy',
        resourceName: 'app-permissions-boundary' }));
    }
  }
}
Aspects.of(app).add(new AppRoles());

    The product CI's verify job fails when a synthesized template has a role without this path and boundary, or a resource type the deploy role cannot create (templates/product-repo/.github/workflows/product-ci.yml).

  4. A role a person created by hand (an older /app/ role without the boundary) is imported with Role.fromRoleArn(this, id, arn, { mutable: false }). A mutable import makes CDK attach an inline policy to it, which the deploy role is refused for a role without the boundary; with mutable: false CDK grants are no-ops, so the person gives that role its permissions.

The deploy role changes only the product's own resources. The deploy role's main allow covers every service, so without deploy-scope-policy.json it could rewrite the code of any Lambda function in the account, or the definition of any state machine, and so run code with that resource's existing role; no iam:PassRole check applies, because the role is not changing. The scope policy limits those changes to resources whose name, or for Amplify whose tag, marks them as the product's. Two choices follow from the AWS Service Authorization Reference:

  • Name prefix, for Lambda, Step Functions, CloudFormation and CodeBuild. The resource name is in the ARN, so a NotResource deny works whether or not an action supports tag conditions, and a name cannot be changed after creation. A tag condition would not be enough here: Lambda needs lambda:TagResource to tag a function at creation, so the deploy role must keep that action, and it could then tag another function project=<product> and change it.
  • Tag, for Amplify. An Amplify app's ARN holds a generated app id, not its name, so the prefix cannot be written in advance. UpdateApp, DeleteApp, UpdateBranch, DeleteBranch, CreateDeployment and StartDeployment support aws:ResourceTag, so they are denied on an app or branch without project=<product>. Adding or removing the project tag is denied on any Amplify resource that does not already carry project=<product>, so the deploy role cannot tag another app into scope. StartJob supports no resource tag, and the product's app has no repository connection and needs no build job, so it is denied everywhere.

What every product stack does for this:

  1. Name each stack <product>-<name> (new Stack(app, 'Claims', { stackName: '<product>-claims' })).

  2. Tag everything: Tags.of(app).add('project', '<product>'). CDK adds the tag to every resource in the app whose type takes tags, including AWS::Amplify::App and AWS::Amplify::Branch; the Amplify rule depends on it.

  3. Give every function, state machine and build project a <product>- name, including the ones CDK creates for itself (custom-resource providers, autoDeleteObjects, BucketDeployment). An aspect does it for all of them:

    import { Aspects, CfnResource, IAspect, Names } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { IConstruct } from 'constructs';

const PRODUCT = '<product>';
const NAME_PROPERTY: Record<string, [string, number]> = {
  'AWS::Lambda::Function': ['FunctionName', 64],
  'AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine': ['StateMachineName', 80],
  'AWS::CodeBuild::Project': ['Name', 150],
};

class ProductNames implements IAspect {
  visit(node: IConstruct): void {
    if (!(node instanceof CfnResource)) return;
    const entry = NAME_PROPERTY[node.cfnResourceType];
    if (!entry) return;
    const [property, maxLength] = entry;
    node.addPropertyOverride(property, `${PRODUCT}-${Names.uniqueResourceName(node,
      { maxLength: maxLength - PRODUCT.length - 1 })}`);
  }
}
Aspects.of(app).add(new ProductNames());

    A function or state machine created without the prefix fails with an access-denied error naming lambda:CreateFunction or states:CreateStateMachine; fix the CDK app, not the policy. A named resource cannot be replaced in place, so a change that needs replacement (for example a new name) needs the old resource removed first.

The sandbox account holds the product stack and nothing else. The scope policy covers the services above. The deploy role can still change resources of every other service in the account, and some of those run code with an existing role (an EC2 instance's user data, an ECS task, an SSM document, a Glue job). Do not create other workloads, other teams' stacks or hand-made functions in the sandbox account; an administrator's own resources (the baseline trail, the CDK bootstrap stack) are the only exceptions.

Service-linked roles are created by a person (setup step 5). OpenSearch Serverless needs one before the first collection.

Secrets. CloudFormation dynamic references to Secrets Manager ({{resolve:secretsmanager:...}}) are resolved with the caller's permissions, which deny GetSecretValue; the boundary denies it to application roles too. If the product needs a secret at run time, the owner adds a narrow allow for that secret's ARN to the boundary.

Bedrock: US inference profiles

Neither model has an in-region endpoint in a US region, so the product calls both through the US geographic inference profiles (owner ruling, 2026-10-14), which route to us-east-1, us-east-2 and us-west-2:

ModelFoundation model idInference profile id
Claude Sonnet 5anthropic.claude-sonnet-5us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
Claude Opus 5.5anthropic.claude-opus-5-5us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5

Only US profiles are allowed, by both the deploy policy and the boundary: the statement DenyInferenceProfilesOutsideTheUS denies a model invocation whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn is not arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/us.*. It is an allow-list, so global., eu., apac. and any profile prefix AWS adds later are denied without being named. A second statement, DenyDirectFoundationModelInvocation, denies invoking a foundation model without a profile, so every model call goes through a US profile, in the sandbox region as elsewhere. Quotas for the profiles are the "Cross-region model inference ... for <model>" service quotas, requested in the sandbox region, one pair per model.

The runtime role grant has three parts. A role that invokes a model through a US profile needs bedrock:InvokeModel (and InvokeModelWithResponseStream if it streams; Converse is authorized as InvokeModel) on:

  1. the inference profile in the sandbox (source) region;
  2. the foundation model in the source region;
  3. the foundation model in every other region the profile routes to,

with parts 2 and 3 limited to calls made through that profile. For Sonnet 5 from a source region <region> (repeat for anthropic.claude-opus-5-5):

[
  { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock:<region>:<account>:inference-profile/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5" },
  { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"],
    "Resource": [
      "arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-5",
      "arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-2::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-5",
      "arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-sonnet-5" ],
    "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn":
      "arn:aws:bedrock:<region>:<account>:inference-profile/us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5" } } }
]

Check the profile's current destination regions with bedrock-claude-advisor before writing the grant; AWS can add regions to a profile.

Why the region deny lets this through. AWS evaluates the foundation model once per candidate destination region, with aws:RequestedRegion set to that region and the condition key bedrock:InferenceProfileArn set to the profile. The region deny in the deploy policy and in the boundary carries "ArnNotLike": {"bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/us.*"}, so it skips exactly the evaluations routed by a US profile; a call without the key, or through any other profile, is still refused outside the sandbox region. The originating call is still locked to the sandbox region: AWS evaluates the inference profile resource with the source region and without that key (AWS Bedrock user guide, "Geographic cross-Region inference", Service Control Policy requirements).

Workbench hosting: Amplify Hosting

The React examiner workbench is a static build hosted on Amplify Hosting. The stack creates the Amplify app and branch (AWS::Amplify::App, AWS::Amplify::Branch) without a repository connection, so no source-control token is stored in AWS. aws-deploy publishes a build with tools/aws-sandbox write amplify create-deployment ..., uploads the zip to the URL it returns, then runs write amplify start-deployment .... The deploy role may change, deploy to and delete only an app and branch tagged project=<product>, may not start a build job, and may pass an /app/ role to amplify.amazonaws.com if the app ever needs a service role. The read role reads jobs, artifacts and domain associations through ReadOnlyAccess; it may not read the app or branch itself, because those responses carry environment variables and basic-auth credentials.

Config point: custom domain and WAF (not set up now). The app uses its default *.amplifyapp.com domain and no web application firewall. To add either later:

  • a custom domain is an AWS::Amplify::Domain resource in the stack; a certificate of your own must be in us-east-1 (ACM for CloudFront), which the region deny refuses, so either let Amplify manage the certificate or have an administrator create it;
  • a firewall is an AWS::WAFv2::WebACL with scope CLOUDFRONT in us-east-1, associated with the Amplify app; the region deny exempts only classic waf:*, so wafv2:* and acm:* in us-east-1 need an exemption in deploy-policy.json, or an administrator creates the web ACL.

ampx (the Amplify Gen 2 CLI) is guarded like cdk: only through tools/aws-sandbox exec from aws-deploy. A Gen 2 backend (ampx sandbox, ampx pipeline-deploy) creates roles outside /app/ without the boundary, which the deploy role refuses; the product's back end is the CDK stack instead.

Tenant keys and tables

The stack creates each tenant's KMS key and DynamoDB table set at deploy time (owner ruling, 2026-10-14). Each tenant key gets the alias alias/<product>-tenant-<tenant>, where <product> is the value that replaces REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCT_NAME; the read role decrypts only through keys with such an alias, so a key without one is unreadable to it. The deploy role keeps kms:PutKeyPolicy and kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion. Each key policy keeps the statement that delegates to IAM in the account, or the roles' IAM policies (including the read role's decrypt) have no effect. Scheduling a key's deletion, or changing a key policy, through tools/aws-sandbox write prompts a person (.claude/settings.json); the same changes made by a cdk deploy through exec are not prompted. A key scheduled for deletion can be recovered with kms cancel-key-deletion during its waiting period (7 to 30 days).

Audit trail and Object Lock
  • The account's baseline trail (created by an administrator, outside the product) cannot be stopped, deleted or updated by the deploy role. Its name replaces REPLACE_WITH_BASELINE_TRAIL_NAME in deploy-policy.json. The product stack's own trail is not covered by that deny, so stack updates and teardown work.
  • The product trail's log bucket uses S3 Object Lock in GOVERNANCE mode with a 1-day default retention in the sandbox (owner ruling, 2026-10-14). The deploy role is denied s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, so it cannot delete or overwrite a locked log version early; an administrator can, with --bypass-governance-retention. Tearing the stack down therefore fails on that bucket until the newest log object is a day old, or until an administrator empties it. Changing the bucket's lock configuration through tools/aws-sandbox write prompts a person.

Synthesizing without credentials

tools/aws-sandbox synth [--dir <cdk app dir>] [cdk args] runs cdk synth with every AWS credential source removed: all AWS_ and BOTO_ variables, the wrapper's profile names and CDK_DEFAULT_* are dropped, AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true is set, and AWS_CONFIG_FILE and AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE point at /dev/null. It refuses --profile and --role-arn, needs no profile configuration, and every agent may run it (.claude/settings.json allows it; the hook lets it through). Use it to read the CloudFormation a change produces: IAM roles and their boundary, trust policies, public endpoints, Object Lock settings. Context lookups fail under it, as in CI; commit cdk.context.json.

Setup (the owner, once per sandbox account)

  1. In local copies of the policy files (never commit the values), replace REPLACE_WITH_SANDBOX_REGION (a US region where the US profiles are offered), REPLACE_WITH_SANDBOX_ACCOUNT_ID, REPLACE_WITH_BASELINE_TRAIL_NAME and (in read-sandbox-data-policy.json, deploy-scope-policy.json and app-permissions-boundary.json) REPLACE_WITH_PRODUCT_NAME: the product's short name, which prefixes the tenant key aliases, the stack names and the function, state machine and build project names, and is the value of the project tag. Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter.

  2. Create the customer managed policy app-permissions-boundary at the path / from iam/app-permissions-boundary.json. The name must match the ARN in deploy-policy.json.

  3. Create the read role: attach ReadOnlyAccess and customer managed policies from iam/read-only-guard-policy.json and, in this sandbox only, iam/read-sandbox-data-policy.json.

  4. Create the deploy role with two customer managed policies, from iam/deploy-policy.json and iam/deploy-scope-policy.json.

  5. Create the OpenSearch Serverless service-linked role, once per account, as an administrator (the deploy role cannot create service-linked roles):

    aws iam create-service-linked-role --aws-service-name observability.aoss.amazonaws.com

    It fails with "has been taken in this account" if the role already exists; that is fine.

  6. Bootstrap CDK once as an administrator, and enable access to Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5.5 in Bedrock.

  7. Let each developer's sandbox identity assume the read and deploy roles: the roles' trust policies name the developers' principals (IAM Identity Center permission sets or IAM users in the sandbox).

Setup (each developer, once per machine)

  1. Add two profiles to ~/.aws/config, one per role, for example:

    [profile sandbox-read]
role_arn = arn:aws:iam::<sandbox-account-id>:role/<read-role-name>
source_profile = <your sandbox login profile>

[profile sandbox-deploy]
role_arn = arn:aws:iam::<sandbox-account-id>:role/<deploy-role-name>
source_profile = <your sandbox login profile>

    Never use the default profile for either; the wrapper refuses it, and refuses one profile used for both roles.

  2. Tell the repository which profiles to use, outside version control: set aws_read_profile, aws_deploy_profile and, if the team's region in .idea-realization/project.yaml does not apply, aws_region in .idea-realization/local.yaml (gitignored; ONBOARDING.md, section 3, step 6). The environment variables IDEA_REALIZATION_AWS_READ_PROFILE, IDEA_REALIZATION_AWS_DEPLOY_PROFILE and IDEA_REALIZATION_AWS_REGION override it for one shell. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/paths.py show prints what this machine resolves and where each value came from.

  3. Remove any default or ambient credentials (the machine rule above), then check: uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe must print OK.

  4. Check the profiles: tools/aws-sandbox whoami prints both profile names and the read role's identity.

What agents may do

  • Reads run freely through tools/aws-sandbox read, with the read role.
  • Every agent may run tools/aws-sandbox synth; it uses no credentials.
  • Only the aws-deploy agent runs tools/aws-sandbox write or exec, with the deploy role. The hook refuses them from any other agent and from the main session.
  • Deleting anything prompts a person for approval each time, and so do scheduling a key's deletion, changing a key policy and changing an Object Lock configuration through write. Organizations, account and billing actions, and IAM changes other than to /app/ roles with the boundary, are refused by the deploy role itself.
  • No agent reads or changes ~/.aws/, sets an AWS_ variable, or runs the AWS CLI, an AWS SDK or a deployment tool (CDK, ampx, SAM, Terraform) outside the wrapper; the hook refuses each of these.

Residual risk

  • The hook is best effort. It matches command text and reads the scripts it can see. A determined or confused agent can still find a command it does not recognise. The IAM roles and the machine rule are the boundary; the hook and the permission rules only keep agents on the intended path.
  • The deploy role can destroy data. Deleting through tools/aws-sandbox write prompts a person, but a deploy script run with tools/aws-sandbox exec, or a stack update that replaces a resource, runs under the deploy role without a prompt. That includes deleting a tenant's table, scheduling a tenant key's deletion and replacing a key policy. Keep nothing in the sandbox that cannot be recreated.
  • The deploy role can change any resource outside the scope policy's services. The scope policy covers Lambda, Step Functions, CloudFormation, CodeBuild and Amplify. Every other service's resources in the account are open to the deploy role, including resources that run code with an existing role. This is safe only while the sandbox account holds the product stack and nothing else (see "The deploy role changes only the product's own resources").
  • The Amplify tag rule is not tested against AWS. It assumes CloudFormation tags a new Amplify app and branch through CreateApp and CreateBranch and calls TagResource only on resources that already carry the tag. If the first deploy fails on amplify:TagResource, tell the owner; the fix is a change to DenyOutsideTheProductAmplifyProjectTag, not removing it.
  • The deploy role can create roles. Each /app/ role is capped by the boundary at about what the deploy role itself may do, so no role it creates gains IAM, account or billing power. Neither the boundary nor any condition key limits a role's trust policy, though: a stack could create an /app/ role that another account may assume. aws-infra-reviewer checks that every trust policy names only AWS service principals.
  • aws-sandbox exec runs whatever it is given (owner ruling, accepted). The guard hook does not stop tools/aws-sandbox exec bash -c '...' from running arbitrary commands with the deploy role's credentials; it checks who calls exec, not what exec runs. This is accepted because the IAM roles are the boundary: anything run that way can do no more than the deploy role allows.
  • The hook does not block the instance metadata service (owner ruling, accepted under the machine rule). A command can reach 169.254.169.254 directly; the hook does not look for it. The machine rule is what makes this safe: there are no instance credentials to find.
  • Agents must not run on an EC2 instance, or on any host that has an instance role or instance-metadata credentials (container task roles included). On such a host the two risks above are no longer covered by the machine rule. tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe reports a reachable metadata service.
  • Read reaches data. ReadOnlyAccess reads object contents and table items, and with read-sandbox-data-policy.json that includes data encrypted with the tenant keys, and Textract results. Keep production or personal data out of the sandbox, and see the warning under "The roles and policies".

Cost guardrails (OPS-007)

Source docs/guides/OPS-007-cost-guardrails.md, whole document

How the team keeps the AWS sandbox's spend visible and bounded: a budget alarm, a daily cost review, tags on every resource, and a teardown checklist. The AWS boundary itself (two roles, the machine rule, the wrapper) is in aws/README.md.

Who can do what

ActionWhoWhy
Create or change a budget, an alert, a cost allocation tag activationThe sandbox administrator (a person with administrator or billing access in the account)aws/iam/deploy-policy.json denies budgets:*, ce:*, cur:*, billing:* and the other billing actions explicitly. The read role has ReadOnlyAccess, which grants no create or update action. .claude/settings.json also asks a person before any tools/aws-sandbox write budgets, ce or cur command.
Read spend and find idle resourcesThe aws-cost-optimizer agent, with the read roleIt runs tools/aws-sandbox read ce get-cost-and-usage ... and describe/list calls. It changes nothing.
Stop or delete a resourceThe aws-deploy agent with a person's approval per deletion, or a personOnly aws-deploy runs write and exec. Every delete, stop or destroy command prompts for approval.
Delete an execution role under /app/The aws-deploy agent, as part of the stack's destroy; the sandbox administrator for a role a person createdThe deploy role creates, changes and deletes /app/ roles that carry the permission boundary (aws/README.md, "The roles and policies"), so the stack's own roles go with the stack. It cannot create, change or delete any other role.

Budget alarm

The sandbox administrator creates it once, before the first deployment, in the AWS Budgets console or with their own administrator credentials. No agent and no sandbox role can.

  1. A monthly cost budget for the sandbox account. The amount is the owner's decision: ask the owner.
  2. Alerts on actual spend at 50%, 80% and 100% of the budget, and on forecast spend at 100%.
  3. Alert recipients: the owner and the team channel's email address, if the channel has one. Ask the owner for the addresses; they are not written in this repository.
  4. Record in the brain that the budget exists, its amount and who receives the alerts, with uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/brain.py new decision ... (no email addresses or account ids in the entry).

When an alert fires, the person who receives it runs the daily cost review below at once and posts the result to the team.

Daily cost review

Once per working day, a validator dispatches the aws-cost-optimizer agent with:

What did the sandbox cost over the last seven days, grouped by service and by the project and owner tags? List resources that are idle or left over from a test, each with its estimated monthly cost and the evidence it is idle, and the change you recommend.

Then:

  1. Post the spend figures and the candidate list to the team.
  2. The owner of each candidate (from its owner tag) either keeps it, with a reason, or asks the aws-deploy agent to remove it. Removal prompts for approval per deletion.
  3. A resource with no owner tag goes to the owner to decide.

Cost Explorer data lags by up to a day, so a resource created this morning may not show yet. Each Cost Explorer API request is billed by AWS; one review a day is a small number of requests. If the agent's ce read is refused, the read role lacks Cost Explorer access: ask the owner, who decides whether the sandbox administrator grants it.

Tags

Every resource the product creates carries two tags:

KeyValue
projectThe product's name. The value is the owner's decision: ask the owner, and use the same value everywhere.
ownerThe handle of the developer whose phase created the resource (the handle identity.py prints).
  • In a CDK app, add both at the app or stack level so every resource inherits them, for example Tags.of(app).add("project", "<project tag>"), and the owner tag per stack.
  • The aws-infra-reviewer agent, reviewing an infrastructure diff, reports resources without the tags the team uses. Name project and owner in its dispatch.
  • Tags only appear in cost reports after the sandbox administrator activates project and owner as cost allocation tags in the Billing console. Activation takes effect for spend from that point on, so do it before the first deployment.

Bedrock spend

  • Model invocations are billed per token. The read role cannot invoke a model, so agents never spend on Bedrock; only the deployed product and people do.
  • Never buy provisioned throughput for a model without the owner's decision: it is billed per hour whether or not it is used.
  • Bedrock spend appears under its own service in the daily review. If it grows faster than the demo rehearsals explain, find the caller before the next rehearsal.

Teardown checklist

Run after the demo, or when a feature's resources are no longer needed. The aws-deploy agent does the removals; each one prompts for approval.

  1. Run the daily cost review once more to get the current list of resources and spend.
  2. Destroy each product stack through the wrapper (for CDK, tools/aws-sandbox exec with the destroy command). Approve each prompt only after reading what it deletes.
  3. Check what a stack deletion leaves behind, because CloudFormation keeps resources whose removal policy is retain: S3 buckets, DynamoDB tables, CloudWatch log groups, ECR repositories and their images, EBS snapshots, KMS keys pending deletion. Remove each one the owner does not want kept.
  4. Check for stacks in DELETE_FAILED (tools/aws-sandbox read cloudformation list-stacks) and resolve each before going on.
  5. The stack destroy in step 2 removes the stack's own roles under /app/. The sandbox administrator deletes any role a person created for the product, and any provisioned throughput or quota increase that has a running cost.
  6. Leave the budget alarm in place until the month's bill has closed.
  7. Run the cost review again the next day: spend per day should fall to near zero. Report any service still charging.
  8. Record what was removed and what was kept, with the reason, in the brain.

Troubleshooting

Common failures, each with its symptom, cause and fix.

Troubleshooting (OPS-008)

Source docs/guides/OPS-008-troubleshooting.md, whole document

Common failures, each with its symptom, its cause and the fix. A fix is given only where the repository's own tools or documents support it; anything else says "ask the owner". Commands run from the control repository's root unless the entry says otherwise.

Two rules apply to every entry:

  • A failing check or hook is a result to fix or report, never a step to retry until it goes quiet.
  • Never commit with --no-verify and never route around a hook. Never force-push dev or main; a feature branch may be force-pushed only with --force-with-lease, after a rebase.

Git and the backlog

A claim push is rejected

  • Symptom. git push of the claim commit to control dev fails with rejected and non-fast-forward or fetch first.

  • Cause. Another developer pushed to control dev after your last pull. Often they claimed a phase too.

  • Fix.

    1. git pull --rebase. If backlog/backlog.yaml conflicts, see the next entry.
    2. Regenerate the catalog (uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/cli.py catalog) and run uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py.
    3. If the check now rejects your claim (overlap with an active peer's systems, deliverables or dependency chain, max_active reached, or another developer's workstream), the claim is not safe: confirm git status --short shows nothing and git log --oneline origin/dev..HEAD shows only your claim commit, then drop it (git reset --hard origin/dev, which then discards only your local claim) and choose another phase. If the log shows another unpushed commit, such as an idea, drop only the claim with git revert or ask for help instead.
    4. If the check passes, git push.

    Source: the session-start skill, step 3.

backlog/backlog.yaml has a merge conflict

  • Symptom. A rebase or pull stops with a conflict in backlog/backlog.yaml.

  • Cause. Two developers edited different phases, or the same updated line, in the same file. This is normal.

  • Fix.

    1. Keep both sides: the peer's phases exactly as they are, and your own phase's edits.
    2. Set the backlog's updated to today.
    3. Never resolve the file with --ours or --theirs; either one deletes a peer's work.
    4. Do not merge docs/catalog.md by hand: regenerate it with uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/cli.py catalog.
    5. If both sides used the same document code, whoever integrates second allocates a new code, renames the file and updates every reference.
    6. Run the check, then git rebase --continue.

    If two phases conflict in product source code, their declared systems or deliverables were wrong. Stop and report it; do not force the merge.

    Source: the session-start skill, "If a rebase conflicts"; plugins/idea-realization/docs/backlog-protocol.md.

The doctor fails

  • Symptom. IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/doctor.py exits 1. Each recorded file is listed with a state.

  • Cause. The doctor compares each file in .idea-realization/install-state.json with the disk. Only some states fail the run:

    • unchanged: matches the record. Does not fail.
    • edited: a data or configuration file people and agents edit by design (backlog/backlog.yaml, docs/codes.yaml, docs/systems.yaml, the idea files, brain/index.md, product.yaml, project.yaml) changed since the scaffold wrote it. This is normal use and does not fail; check.py validates the content.
    • absent: a recorded directory that git ignores, such as .idea-realization/staging/, is not there. A fresh clone never has it. Does not fail.
    • stale: a schema copy under .idea-realization/schemas/ differs from the plugin's own copy. Fails.
    • unrecorded: a schema copy matches the plugin's, but the record still holds an older hash (the copy was updated by hand). Fails.
    • drifted: a schema copy that this plugin version no longer ships differs from the record, or .gitignore changed since the scaffold changed it with consent. Fails.
    • missing: a recorded file, or a recorded directory git does not ignore, was removed. Fails.

  • Fix.

    • stale or unrecorded: run the command the doctor's line names, for example IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/scaffold.py --feature backlog --refresh-schemas. It replaces the copy with the plugin's file (or only records the current hash when the content already matches) and never touches data files. Add --dry-run first to see what it would do. Commit the refreshed schema and install-state.json together.
    • missing: run the scaffold again for that feature, for example IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/scaffold.py --feature partition. It writes only what is missing and never overwrites.
    • drifted: ask the owner.
    • edited and absent: no action.

    Source: the doctor and scaffold skills (plugins/idea-realization/skills/).

A hook refuses a commit or a command
  • Symptom A: pre-commit. git commit stops. The hook (tools/git-hooks/pre-commit) runs tools/check_confidential.py and then check.py; the output is either check_confidential: FAILED with one line per violation, or the check's error lines.
  • Fix A.
    • Confidential violation: remove the identifier from the file, git add it again (the check reads the staged content, not the file on disk), and commit. A file under .private/ must not be tracked: git rm --cached <file>.
    • Check failure: fix what it names. A stale catalog is fixed by uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/cli.py catalog and staging the result.
    • If you believe the check itself is wrong, stop and report it to the owner.
  • Symptom B: AWS guard. A Bash command is refused with aws_guard: refused: <reason>.
  • Fix B. The reason names the rule. Use tools/aws-sandbox read ... for reads. A create or update goes to the aws-deploy agent. Never set an AWS_ variable or touch ~/.aws/. If the guard blocks a command that is legitimate, report it to the owner; do not rephrase the command to get past it.
  • Symptom C: permission rule. An edit to CLAUDE.md, ideas/ideas.jsonl or anything under .private/ is denied.
  • Fix C. These are denied on purpose. CLAUDE.md changes only with the owner's approval of the exact text. The idea log changes only through /idea-realization:idea (scripts/idea.py).
check.py reports files from the wrong repository

  • Symptom. check.py (or paths.py, doctor.py) reports a root: that is not this repository, or errors about files that are not here.

  • Cause. The scripts take the root from --root, then IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT, then git rev-parse --show-toplevel of the directory the command runs in, then CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR (which comes first only when it is a folder inside that working tree and the command runs inside it). When this repository sits inside another git repository's working tree and the command runs outside Claude Code's project directory, or the command runs from another directory, the later sources resolve to the wrong place.

  • Fix. Set the root on the one command, from this repository's root:

    IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT=$PWD uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/paths.py   # root: must be this repository

    or pass --root <path> to the one command. Do not export the variable: with it set in the shell, uv run pytest fails, because the plugin tests build their own temporary repositories (OPS-001, section 7). If you exported it, unset IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT before running tests.

Pull requests and CI

gh cannot reach the repository

  • Symptom. session-close stops before merging and reports that gh cannot reach a repository whose origin is on GitHub: gh repo view --json nameWithOwner fails in that worktree because gh is not logged in, its token expired, the organization's single sign-on is not authorized for it, or you have no access to the repository.

  • Cause. session-close merges a repository whose origin is on GitHub only through a pull request. When gh cannot reach it, the skill stops and reports; it never falls back to a local merge for a GitHub origin, because control dev has no pull-request rule and would accept a merge with no pull request. The local git merge --no-ff is only for a repository with no origin, or whose origin is a path on this machine: product.py merge-route --checkout <worktree> prints local for those, and treats every other origin as hosted.

  • Fix.

    1. Fix the login: gh auth login, or authorize the token for the organization's single sign-on. Check with gh auth status and gh repo view --json nameWithOwner in both worktrees.
    2. If you lack write access to either repository, ask the owner for it.
    3. Run session-close again. Never merge or push to dev by hand to get past the stop.

    Source: the session-close skill, step 6, "Which path applies".

A pull request merge is refused by --match-head-commit

  • Symptom. gh pr merge <n> --merge --match-head-commit <sha> fails and the pull request stays open.

  • Cause. The branch's head is no longer the commit the gating review judged: a commit was pushed after the review. --match-head-commit makes GitHub refuse exactly this case.

  • Fix.

    1. Do not merge without the flag, and do not pass the new head's hash in place of the reviewed one.
    2. See what changed: git fetch and git log <reviewed_commit>..origin/agent/<phase-id>.
    3. If the new commits belong in the phase, re-run the verification and a new gating review of the new head, record it as a second verdict (...-2.json), then merge with the new reviewed_commit.
    4. If they do not belong (pushed by mistake), ask the owner before rewriting the branch.

    Source: the session-close skill, merge steps.

The required check verify is pending or failed
  • Symptom. A product pull request to dev or main cannot be merged: gh pr checks <n> shows verify as pending, failed or missing.
  • Cause and fix.
    • Pending: wait with gh pr checks <n> --watch.
    • Failed: read the failing step with gh run view <run id> --log-failed. Fix it on the branch and push. The head has moved, so the gating review must judge the new head before the merge (previous entry).
    • Missing or never starts: the workflow file (ci_workflow in .idea-realization/product.yaml, normally product-ci.yml) is not on the branch, or its job is not named verify, or GitHub Actions is not enabled for the repository. Check the first two in the repository. Enabling Actions and changing the ruleset are the owner's: ask the owner.
CI fails with "The repository secret DENY_LIST is not set"

  • Symptom. The Private-content check step (control) or Confidential check step (product) fails with that message.

  • Cause. The workflow has no deny-list to check against. A missing secret fails the run in both repositories by design. A pull request from a fork never receives secrets, so it always fails here.

  • Fix. The owner sets the secret: gh secret set DENY_LIST --repo <org>/<repo> < .private/deny-list.txt, then re-runs the job. Do not remove or weaken the step. A fork pull request is recreated as a branch in the repository instead.

    Source: docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, section 7.

Control CI cannot read the product repository

  • Symptom. In control CI, the Product repository settings step fails with "The repository secret PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN is not set" or "The product repository is not named", or the Check out the product repository (read-only) step fails with an authentication error, Bad credentials, Repository not found or could not read Username.

  • Cause.

    • The secret PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN is not set on the control repository, or the run is a pull request from a fork, which never receives secrets.
    • Neither the repository variable PRODUCT_GITHUB nor github: in .idea-realization/product.yaml names the product repository.
    • The token has expired or been revoked, is still pending an organization's approval, or does not include the product repository with Contents read-only. GitHub answers a token that cannot see a private repository with Repository not found, not with a permissions error.

  • Fix. The owner creates a new token with the settings in docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md (section 7), sets it with gh secret set PRODUCT_READ_TOKEN --repo <org>/<control-repo>, deletes the old token, and re-runs the job (gh run rerun <run id>). For an unnamed product the owner sets gh variable set PRODUCT_GITHUB --repo <org>/<control-repo> --body <org>/<repo>. Do not remove the step, unset IDEA_REALIZATION_REQUIRE_PRODUCT, or widen the token's permissions. A fork pull request is recreated as a branch in the repository instead.

    Source: docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, section 7.

apply_rulesets.sh says the main merger has no access

  • Symptom. tools/github/apply_rulesets.sh stops with error: User '<login>' has no access to <org>/<repo> (or Team '<org>/<team-slug>'), and says nothing was changed on GitHub.

  • Cause. The script gives the bypass on main and on demo-* tag creation only to an actor that already has access to the repository. GitHub answered 404 to the access check: the user is not a collaborator, the team does not have the repository, or the name is misspelled.

  • Fix. Check the third argument's spelling. If it is right, grant the account or team access to the repository first (a team needs at least write access), then run the script again.

    Source: docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, section 9.

A merge into main is refused

  • Symptom. A pull request from dev to main cannot be merged, or a push to main is rejected, with a message that the ref is protected by a ruleset (for example "Cannot update this protected ref").

  • Cause. Only the owner can update main (the update rule in control-main.json and product-main.json, with the owner as the only bypass actor), and only through a pull request.

  • Fix. Ask the owner to merge the release pull request. If the owner's own merge is refused, the rulesets were applied without the main merger or with the wrong one: the owner re-runs tools/github/apply_rulesets.sh with the right third argument.

    Source: docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, section 9.

A push of a demo-* tag is refused

  • Symptom. git push origin demo-rc-<n> (or demo-final) is rejected with a message that the ref is protected by a ruleset (for example "Cannot create ref due to creations being restricted" or "Cannot update this protected ref").

  • Cause. Two rulesets cover refs/tags/demo-*. demo-tags-create restricts creation to the owner, the only bypass actor. demo-tags-protect refuses moving or deleting an existing tag for everyone, the owner included.

  • Fix.

    • You are not the owner: do not retry and do not push the tag under another name. Ask the owner to create and push it (OPS-006, "Release candidate", step 3). Delete your local tag with git tag -d <tag> so it does not differ from the one the owner pushes.
    • The owner's push of a new tag is refused: the rulesets were applied without the main merger or with the wrong one. Re-run tools/github/apply_rulesets.sh with the right third argument; the bypass list of demo-tags-create must show one actor with bypass_mode always.
    • The tag already exists on the remote: it cannot be moved or deleted. Make the next release candidate, demo-rc-<n+1>, instead.

    Source: docs/guides/OPS-001-branching-and-ci.md, section 9, "Who creates demo-* tags".

AWS

AccessDenied on iam:CreateRole

  • Symptom. A deployment fails with an access-denied error naming iam:CreateRole, iam:PutRolePolicy or another IAM change.

  • Cause. The deploy role creates and changes IAM roles only under the path /app/ and only with the permission boundary app-permissions-boundary attached (aws/iam/deploy-policy.json, statements AllowChangingAppRolesOnlyUnderTheBoundary, DenyAppRoleChangesWithoutTheBoundary and DenyEveryIamChangeOutsideAppRoles).
