The stack creates a role without the path or the boundary, or a resource the deploy role never creates (a customer managed policy, user, group or service-linked role), or a CDK grant attaches a policy to a person-created role imported as mutable.

  • Fix.

    1. Synthesize with tools/aws-sandbox synth --dir <app dir> and find the role in cdk.out/ that lacks "Path": "/app/" or PermissionsBoundary.
    2. Apply the CDK settings in aws/README.md ("CDK settings every product stack uses"): the @aws-cdk/core:permissionsBoundary context key and the aspect that sets the path. Import a person-created role with Role.fromRoleArn(this, id, arn, { mutable: false }).
    3. A service-linked role (for example OpenSearch Serverless's) is created once by the sandbox administrator (aws/README.md, "Setup (the owner, once per sandbox account)", step 5).
    4. Deploy again with aws-deploy.

    Source: aws/README.md, "What the deploy role can and cannot deploy".

A script that imports an AWS SDK is refused
  • Symptom. python lambdas/handler.py or node infra/bin/app.js is refused with aws_guard: refused: the script ... uses boto3 (or @aws-sdk, aws-cdk-lib).
  • Cause. The hook refuses running any script by path that loads an AWS SDK, so product code that calls Bedrock or Textract cannot be run directly.
  • Fix. Run tests through the test runner (uv run pytest, npm test, npx vitest), which the hook does not inspect for SDK imports, with the AWS clients mocked. To see a CDK app's CloudFormation, use tools/aws-sandbox synth. Only aws-deploy runs SDK code against AWS, through tools/aws-sandbox exec.
CDK cannot assume its bootstrap roles

  • Symptom. cdk deploy (run through tools/aws-sandbox exec) fails because it could not assume a role named like cdk-...-deploy-role-..., or reports access denied on sts:AssumeRole.

  • Cause. The default CDK synthesizer assumes bootstrap roles, and the deploy role denies sts:AssumeRole.

  • Fix. Use CliCredentialsStackSynthesizer in the product's CDK app, so CDK deploys with the deploy profile's own credentials. The account is bootstrapped once by an administrator; if it is not, ask the owner.

    Source: aws/README.md, "What the deploy role can and cannot deploy", "CDK settings every product stack uses", item 1.

Bedrock model access is denied
  • Symptom. The deployed product's call to Bedrock fails with AccessDeniedException, or with a validation error saying the model id needs an inference profile.
  • Cause. One of: the account has no access to that model in the region; the model is called by its model id (anthropic.claude-sonnet-5) where it must be called through the US inference profile (us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5), since neither Claude Sonnet 5 nor Claude Opus 5.5 has an in-region endpoint in a US region; the product's execution role under /app/ lacks one of the three parts of the inference-profile grant (aws/README.md, "Bedrock: US inference profiles"); or the call uses a profile other than a us. one (global., eu., apac. ...), which the deploy policy and the boundary deny.
  • Fix.
    1. Dispatch bedrock-claude-advisor to list the models and inference profiles the account can call, and the right id for the product's call. It never invokes a model.
    2. Enabling model access is the sandbox administrator's. A missing grant is fixed in the stack that creates the execution role, and deployed by aws-deploy.
    3. Agents cannot test a call: the read role denies bedrock:InvokeModel and Converse. The advisor gives the smallest test request for a person to run.
A ce, budget or billing command is refused

See the cost guardrails guide (OPS-007): budgets and billing are the sandbox administrator's.

Local development

The dev server's port is already in use
  • Symptom. Starting a dev server fails with EADDRINUSE or address already in use.
  • Cause. Another worktree's server, often a peer agent's on the same machine, holds the port.
  • Fix. Find the holder with ss -ltnp | grep :<port> (or lsof -i :<port>). Do not stop a process you did not start. Start your server on a free port, given explicitly (for example --port <free port>). The session-start skill, step 5, requires choosing a port explicitly rather than assuming the default is free. Whether the team assigns port ranges per developer is the owner's decision: ask the owner.

Not covered here

If a failure is not listed, record it with the brain skill as a lesson once it is solved, so the next person finds it, and tell the owner if it should be added here.

Day-one checklist

The first-day setup from the onboarding page, once per machine, in order, then the prompts to paste into Claude Code for the first session and each working mode.

Onboarding

Source ONBOARDING.md, from “3. First-day checklist” up to “4. Claim your workstream”

3. First-day checklist

Do these once per machine, in order. Run uv run python tools/onboard_check.py at any point: it prints OK or FIX for each item it can check, and the commands it cannot run for you.

Run every command below from the control repository's root. The scripts find the root from git, so none of them needs IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT. Do not export that variable: with it set, uv run pytest fails (OPS-001, section 7). When a script does resolve the wrong root, set it on that one command only (OPS-008, "check.py reports files from the wrong repository").

  1. Install the tools.

    • uv (Python runs through it).
    • Claude Code (the claude command).
    • The GitHub CLI gh, then gh auth login to the team's GitHub organization. session-close opens and merges pull requests with gh, so it must be authenticated, and you need write access to both repositories. Ask the owner if you were not invited to both.
    • The AWS CLI v2 (the aws command). tools/aws-sandbox runs it; you never run aws yourself.
    • Node.js and npm, for product work: each product worktree runs npm install, and tools/aws-sandbox synth runs the CDK CLI from the product's node_modules.

  2. Clone the control repository and enter it. Ask the owner for its URL.

    git clone <control repository URL>
cd <control repository>
git checkout dev
uv sync --extra dev

  3. Install the git hooks: git config core.hooksPath tools/git-hooks. The pre-commit hook runs the private-content check and the repository check. Install it before your first commit.

  4. Get the deny-list from the owner and save it as .private/deny-list.txt in the primary checkout. .private/ is gitignored. The pre-commit hook refuses any commit that contains a listed identifier; without the list it skips that part of the check. Never copy anything from it into a tracked file.

  5. Set your git identity and register it.

    • git config user.email <your work email>.

    • Add yourself to the owners map in docs/systems.yaml: the key is your handle (lower-case letters and digits, starting with a letter, at most 16 characters), the value lists your git email. The handle is how every claim, idea and brain entry names you. A work email here is expected; it is not a confidential identifier.

      owners:
  ana:
    description: Ana, user interface workstream.
    emails: ["<handle>@<work-domain>"]

    • Check it: uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/identity.py prints your handle.

    • Commit only docs/systems.yaml directly on control dev and push at once (the team workflow guide, OPS-005, section 1, treats it as bookkeeping). The hook from step 3 checks this commit. If the push is rejected, someone pushed first: git pull --rebase origin dev, then push again.

  6. Write your machine's configuration: copy .idea-realization/local.example.yaml to .idea-realization/local.yaml (gitignored) and fill in what you know now. Delete a key you do not set; a value left as REPLACE-WITH-... counts as unset, and onboard_check reports it.

    • handle: your handle from step 5.
    • control_remote and product_remote: the git URLs of the two repositories, from the owner. They are not tracked, because a URL can name a confidential organization. control_github and product_github (<org>/<repo>) are optional and used by gh.
    • product_root comes in step 9, and aws_read_profile, aws_deploy_profile and, if the team's default does not apply, aws_region in step 8. Leave them until then.

    local.yaml is where this team keeps every per-machine value. A value is taken from, in order: a command-line flag, an IDEA_REALIZATION_<KEY> environment variable, local.yaml, a saved plugin option, the tracked .idea-realization/project.yaml or product.yaml, and the plugin's default. Do not set plugin options for this team: local.yaml covers every key. uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/paths.py show prints every value and where it came from.

  7. Scaffold and check the repository.

    uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/scaffold.py --feature all   # never overwrites a file
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/doctor.py                   # must exit 0
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py                    # must exit 0

  8. Set up AWS as aws/README.md, "Setup (each developer, once per machine)", describes: two named profiles in ~/.aws/config, one for the read role and one for the deploy role, and no default profile or AWS_ credential variables. Ask the owner what your sandbox login profile is (the source_profile the two profiles use). Put the two profile names, and the region if it differs from the team's, in local.yaml. Then:

    uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe   # must print OK
tools/aws-sandbox whoami                           # both profile names and the read identity

    If your sandbox access is not ready yet, skip this step and come back to it before your first phase that touches AWS. Until then onboard_check keeps reporting FIX for the AWS lines; that is expected, and the rest of the checklist does not depend on it.

  9. Clone the product repository beside the control repository, set product_root in local.yaml to it, and check that it is the right repository:

    git clone <product repository URL> ../<product>
git -C ../<product> checkout dev
uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/product.py verify   # prints "origin: matches"

  10. Start Claude Code in the control repository's primary checkout:

    claude

    The first time, Claude Code asks whether you trust the folder. Accept: the project settings (.claude/settings.json) load the plugin only in a trusted folder. /start then exists; if it does not, run /plugin and check that idea-realization@idea-realization-team is enabled.

    There is no product worktree yet, so nothing else is added at launch. session-start creates one when you claim a phase, and you add it then with /add-dir (section 6, step 4).

    The session banner prints your handle, the product checkout and the days to the demo. A line that reads not set on this machine or (unavailable: ...) is a setup step above that is not done yet.

Finish by running uv run python tools/onboard_check.py until it exits 0, or until only the AWS lines of step 8 remain while your sandbox access is pending.

Day-one prompts (OPS-010)

Source docs/guides/OPS-010-day-one-prompts.md, whole document

Prompts a developer pastes into Claude Code for the common sessions: the first session on a new machine, planning, implementing a phase, asking for a review, and release day. Each prompt follows CLAUDE.md and the guides it names; where a prompt and a guide differ, the guide wins. The one-page command list per mode is in the mode cheat sheets (OPS-009).

How to use these prompts

  • Start Claude Code in the control repository's primary checkout with claude, and trust the folder so the project settings load the plugin (ONBOARDING §3 step 10). Then paste one prompt.
  • Text in <angle brackets> is yours to fill in before you paste. Each prompt fits one session.
  • Where a prompt runs the product's tests, it runs them in the product worktree, as the session-start skill §5 and the implementing guide (OPS-003, step 3.6) state.
  • The plugin's skills run by their short name, such as /start; the long form /start always works (ONBOARDING.md §1, "Skill names"). Each prompt names the skill, and the agent invokes it.

1. First session: set up the machine, then /start

Paste this once per machine, on your first day. It does not claim any work.

This is my first session in this team's control repository. I am a new developer, and my handle
will be <handle>.

1. Read CLAUDE.md and ONBOARDING.md in full before doing anything else.
2. Run `uv run python tools/onboard_check.py` and show me its output as printed. For each FIX
   line, take me through the matching step in ONBOARDING.md section 3, one step at a time, in
   order. I run anything that needs a credential or a URL myself. Do not make up a URL, an email,
   an AWS profile name or a deny-list entry; ask me for each one with AskUserQuestion.
3. Never read or write anything under .private/ or ~/.aws/ unless I tell you to. I will save the
   deny-list myself.
4. The only commit you may make today is my `owners` entry in docs/systems.yaml (ONBOARDING
   section 3, step 5), and later my workstream claim in docs/workstreams.yaml (section 4). Each
   goes directly on control `dev`, is pushed at once, and contains nothing else. Show me the diff
   and ask before you commit.
5. Repeat `uv run python tools/onboard_check.py` until it exits 0, or until only the AWS lines of
   step 8 remain while my sandbox access is pending. Show me the final output.
6. Then run the `start` skill and stop at its mode question.

When something I asked for conflicts with CLAUDE.md, say so and follow CLAUDE.md. If a document is
wrong, quote the passage and tell me. Do not edit CLAUDE.md.

2. Planning mode

For the person who turns ideas into an approved plan and phases. The planning guide (OPS-002) reserves every gate to the owner. Someone who is not the owner stops at each gate.

Planning session. I am <handle>; the owner is <owner handle>.

1. Run the `start` skill and choose Planning. Read docs/guides/OPS-002-planning-mode.md in full.
   Follow it step by step and ask me before each step.
2. First, I pull: `git pull --rebase origin dev` in the control primary checkout. Do not run the
   pull yourself. Then load what is already decided:
   `uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/brain.py load --kind decision`.
3. Today's work: <record these ideas: ... | triage the open ideas | partition the triaged ideas |
   plan accepted track <track> | split approved plan <PLAN-code>>.
4. Run scripts from the control root; they find it from git. Never export IDEA_REALIZATION_ROOT:
   if a script resolves the wrong root, set it on that one command only. Dispatch every agent
   by its own name (idea-triage, idea-planner, plan-adversary, phase-splitter, batch-validator).
   Never dispatch a general-purpose agent in place of one.
5. Reserve every document code with the `next-code` skill. Never pick a code by reading a
   directory.
6. Idea commits go directly on control `dev` and are pushed at once. Everything else (partition
   record, requirement, plan, backlog phases, batches, catalog) goes in a control worktree on
   `agent/<handle>-<slug>` and reaches `dev` through a pull request.
7. Stop at each owner gate and tell me what the owner has to decide: accepting the partition,
   approving the plan, ranking next_up, composing a batch and assigning phases. No agent makes
   those decisions, and you do not.
8. Before any commit, `uv run plugins/idea-realization/scripts/check.py` must exit 0. Show me its
   output.

3. Implementing a phase

For building one phase. The first form starts a new phase; the second resumes one this developer already claimed.

3a. Start a phase
Implementing session. I am <handle>. <Optional: the owner assigned me <phase-id>.>

1. Run the `start` skill and choose Implementing. Read
   docs/guides/OPS-003-implementing-mode.md in full and follow its steps in order.
2. First, I pull: `git pull --rebase origin dev` in both primary checkouts (control and product).
   Do not run the pull yourself.
3. Load context with the `brain` skill for the phase's subject.
4. Run the `backlog` skill. Take the first ready phase in next_up order, preferring one with
   `owner: <handle>`. If the check is red, stop: nothing is claimed on a red backlog.
5. Run the `session-start` skill. It asks before claiming. When it asks, show me the phase's
   scope, acceptance, verification, systems and deliverables, its Conflicts column, and whether
   its deliverables are in my workstream. The claim goes directly on control `dev` and is pushed
   at once.
6. After the claim, tell me the exact `/add-dir <product worktree dir>/<phase-id>` line to run.
   Install the product worktree's own environment and run the product's tests there once,
   before any change. Keep that output.
7. Build only inside the phase's declared systems and deliverables. A path that starts with
   `product:` is in the product worktree. If the work needs a file outside them, stop and tell me.
   Commit small diffs on agent/<phase-id>. Rebase onto origin/dev; never merge dev in.
8. Choose a free port yourself for any dev server.
9. Every AWS command goes through tools/aws-sandbox. Ask bedrock-claude-advisor before writing a
   Bedrock call. Have aws-infra-reviewer review any infrastructure diff before it is deployed.
   Only the aws-deploy agent deploys.
10. Record any new ask as an idea with the `idea` skill. Do not fold it into this phase.
11. When I stop, run the `checkpoint` skill from the control worktree. It records the control
    repository only: add the product branch's tip and the product verification output to the
    record yourself.
3b. Resume a claimed phase
Resume <phase-id>. I claimed it earlier; it is active with my agent id.

1. Run the `start` skill and choose Implementing. I run `git pull --rebase origin dev` in both
   primary checkouts first.
2. Do not claim again. Read the phase in backlog/backlog.yaml on control `dev`, then its latest
   session record in the control worktree <worktree dir>/<phase-id>, and its next_action.
3. Check that both agent/<phase-id> worktrees exist and say where each branch tip is
   (`git -C <path> log -1 --oneline`). If one is missing, stop and tell me. Do not recreate it
   from memory.
4. Add the product worktree with /add-dir. Rebase both branches onto origin/dev and rerun the
   product's tests in the product worktree before changing anything.
5. Then continue from step 7 of the start-a-phase prompt.

4. Asking for a review

There is no review skill (OPS-004, "Reviewing a peer's ready branch"). Your own phase's gating review runs inside session-close. A review of a peer's branch is done by hand and does not replace their gating review.

4a. Close your own phase (the gating review)
Close <phase-id>.

1. Run the phase's verification list first: each command in the product worktree, except those
   that start with `control:`, which run in the control worktree. Show me the real output. A
   failing check is a result; report it, do not retry it until it passes.
2. If any acceptance condition does not hold, stop. Run the `checkpoint` skill and tell me what
   remains.
3. If every condition holds, record what the next session should know with the `brain` skill,
   in the control worktree, so the entry reaches `dev` in the control pull request. Then run the
   `session-close` skill. Its gating review uses a fresh phase-adversary agent (or validator-code
   for a narrow change against one requirement), never a general-purpose agent and never a fork
   of this session. Give the reviewer the brief the skill specifies and none of my explanations.
4. Show me the verdict's first line and every finding. Fix each finding or ask me to accept it.
   After a fix, the new HEAD gets a fresh review. Two rejects on the same finding: stop and tell me.
5. Merge only on a pass, with merge commits, control first and then product once `verify` passes.
   Confirm that the product merge commit's second parent is the reviewed commit. Then write the
   completion commit on control `dev` and push it. If session-close stops because `gh` cannot
   reach a repository, tell me; never merge or push to `dev` by hand to get past it.
6. Never commit with --no-verify. A failing hook is a finding to fix or report.
4b. Review a peer's pushed branch
Validating session. Review <peer handle>'s branch for <phase-id>. This review is advice for the
peer and does not replace their gating review in session-close.

1. Run the `start` skill and choose Validating. Read docs/guides/OPS-004-validating-mode.md,
   section "Reviewing a peer's ready branch", and follow its six steps.
2. `git fetch origin` in each primary checkout and confirm that origin/agent/<phase-id> exists. If
   it does not, stop and tell me.
3. Create detached review worktrees outside the repositories, at the pushed commit, so the peer's
   branch never moves. Install the product worktree's own environment there.
4. Dispatch a fresh phase-adversary agent with the phase's scope, acceptance, verification and
   deliverables from control `dev`, both review worktree paths with the range origin/dev...HEAD,
   and the requirement and plan paths. Give it nothing the peer wrote to explain the work.
5. Show me the full reply with the reviewed commit, so I can send it to the peer. Commit nothing
   on the peer's branch.
6. Change nothing you review.
7. When I confirm, remove both review worktrees with `git worktree remove`.

5. Release day

Demo 2026-11-05, freeze 2026-11-03 (OPS-006). Only the owner merges into main and creates tags. Each prompt below states which role uses it. The release developer and the validator should be different people.

5a. Release developer: release candidate and deploy
Release session. I am the release developer for demo-rc-<n>. Read
docs/guides/OPS-006-demo-day-runbook.md in full and follow it.

1. In both repositories, in that order (control, then product), prepare the release pull request
   from dev to main with the command in OPS-006, "Release candidate", step 1. Show me the command
   and the body before you run it. In the product repository, wait for `verify` with
   `gh pr checks <number> --watch`.
2. Stop there. The owner merges the release pull requests and creates the demo-rc-<n> tags. Do
   not merge into main, and do not create, move or push a tag.
3. After the owner tags, check the machine: `uv run python tools/check_aws_machine.py --probe`
   must print OK, then run `tools/aws-sandbox whoami`.
4. Check out the tag in a separate detached product worktree (OPS-006, "Local deployment",
   step 2). Do not use any working branch.
5. Dispatch the aws-deploy agent with the worktree path, the tag, the product's deploy command and
   the smoke test's first check as its verification. It shows a diff or change set before it
   applies anything. Before any prompt to delete appears, tell me exactly what will be deleted. A
   refused prompt means stop.
6. Keep the deploy report, with what was created or updated and the verification output, where
   the owner asks.
5b. Validator: smoke test
Validating session. Smoke test demo-rc-<n> (or demo-final) as deployed. I am the validator, not
the person who deployed it.

1. Read docs/guides/OPS-006-demo-day-runbook.md, sections "Smoke test" and "On the day".
2. Run each check of the written smoke test in the product repository, in order. Record pass or
   fail for each check with its real output or a screenshot.
3. Dispatch the aws-ops-inspector agent to read the deployed resources' state and recent errors,
   and add its output to the record.
4. Change nothing on the deployed stack. A failed check becomes a fix: record it as an idea with
   the `idea` skill, and the owner registers a phase for it.
